Mr. Chairman, I have a question to put to the minister. I have been absent from Ottawa for a few days, but I read the minister's initial statement to the committee. Anything that has been done to increase Canadian exports to other countries is most welcome. My remarks are related to the field of industrial as well as agricultural products.
The contracts for the sale of Canadian products abroad, whether grain sales through the Canadian wheat board or sales of steel produced in Canadian mills, are contracts signed by the agencies involved. The minister's department, through the trade commissioners, has taken a very active interest in promoting Canadian trade and exports of all kinds. I should like from the minister an indication of what is involved in a general sense in trade commissioners promoting the sale of Canadian products. If it is possible for him to do so I should like the minister to inform the committee what part the trade commissioners play in the sale of grain, and whether any part was played by the commissioners in the preliminary stages preceding the signing of the grain agreement recently negotiated with China.

subsubtopic: RECOMMENDATION OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS RESPECTING LOCATION
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman, I shall be glad to answer that question. In many cases our trade commissioners make the initial contacts for Canadian firms which are anxious to sell in foreign markets. The trade commissioners give Canadian firms preliminary information regarding freight rates, tariffs and
Supply-Trade and Commerce information concerning other pertinent matters before a deal is consummated. If necessary the trade commissioners act as interpreters between the Canadian businessman and the foreign customer. As I said yesterday in committee, the trade commissioners do everything except actually sign the deal. They may be compared with a catalyst in a chemical reaction which does everything except actually make the reaction.
Regarding sales of wheat, to which the hon. member for Assiniboia has referred, our trade commissioners are very active in the preliminary contacts with the government agencies of the foreign governments concerned. They act on behalf of the wheat board in the same way they do on behalf of Canadian business companies. In the case of the recent deal signed with China, our trade commissioners were very active indeed in making the initial contact and helping line up the deal.

subsubtopic: RECOMMENDATION OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS RESPECTING LOCATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I very much appreciate getting that information from the minister, because it means that the specific details of any contract, whether it be entered into by a private company or by the Canadian wheat board, are signed by the company involved. But as the minister himself said, the trade commissioners, as I would think they should, do everything in the promotion of these sales except sign on the dotted line.
I was very much interested in the statement about the sale of additional grain to China. The minister has at this time referred to the role his department played in this contract, as well as having referred to it on April 28. With regard to this sale of Canadian grain, as with a private sale if it should have been a private sale by any company, I wish to make it clear that we are in favour of this kind of increased trade in non-military products, no matter what the political complexion of the government involved.
If we are to hope that in the future these governments which are so much different than ours may come closer to the road to freedom, the way to encourage this, in our judgment, is to undertake this kind of agreement and negotiate a trade in non-strategic materials. We are happy that this is done with China, with Cuba or any other country, even though we may object very violently to the particular form of government in those countries.
A great deal has been said about this grain deal which was announced in the house on May 2. I read the reports in the western newspapers. I do not think any transaction has been undertaken in the field of trade which has been given more widespread or
4326	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce more favourable publicity than this particular transaction. I read all the reports I was able to find in all the different newspapers. I read that it was a sale of 186 million bushels of wheat and 46 million bushels of barley; that the sale was worth $362 million, and it would take place between June 1 this year and December, 1963. In my comments I was just as much in favour of it as any hon. member in this house. The president of the Saskatchewan wheat pool went so far as to say that this solved the grain problem for the farmers; that this would mean that the surplus of grain would be moved off the farms.
I was astounded to read the provisions of this agreement when I went over them in Hansard as set forth by the minister. I have never seen an instance in my experience in the house-and I think other members of parliament will agree-when the press gallery failed to see a joker in an announcement; and there is a big joker in this announcement.

subsubtopic: RECOMMENDATION OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS RESPECTING LOCATION
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speechtext:
This is a firm agreement for the sale of 28 million bushels of wheat, 17 million bushels of barley and 1.5 million bushels transferred or related into flour. After that there is no firm agreement. There is certainly no firm agreement on behalf of China or the China Resources Company. As far as the future is concerned, these are the minister's words:
Each future contract will be negotiated in respect to price and quantity.
I put it to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that there is no guarantee, in this agreement which has been announced, for sales beyond the 28 million bushels of wheat. This is not what it has been dressed up to mean, a firm sale within a period from now to December, 1963, of these huge quantities of grain. I think in making the announcement the minister was really putting his public relations people to work, because they have blown up and exaggerated this agreement almost beyond recognition.
There is something firm in the agreement. It is firm, as I understand it. I should like to read the agreement; I think it should be produced.

subsubtopic: RECOMMENDATION OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS RESPECTING LOCATION
speechtext: What good will that do you?

subsubtopic: RECOMMENDATION OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS RESPECTING LOCATION
speechtext:
As I read the statement there is something firm in it. I will read the minister's words:
We have committed ourselves to provide up to six million tons of barley, wheat and flour.
That is the main agreement. Canada has been committed to provide but China is not committed to purchase that quantity, to say


nothing about the price. We had an experience in the uranium industry. Letters of intent were exchanged which seemed pretty firm. There is nothing nearly as firm in this agreement. I cannot see, from reading this agreement anything as firm as there was in the uranium deal. The uranium deal is not too firm at the moment, but it was certainly much firmer to begin with than this agreement.

subsubtopic: RECOMMENDATION OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS RESPECTING LOCATION
speechtext: This sounds like sour grapes.

We should like to hear from the minister on behalf of the government whether or not $362 million worth of Canadian grain will be sold, and I say there is no such assurance and no such agreement. In the past this government has turned down an opportunity to sell on a contract basis, on a loan and partial cash basis, any part of 586 million bushels of grain, an opportunity which was picked up by the United States and the grain provided by the United States. I am in favour of selling to communist China; I have made that clear, but I do not think we have to lean over backward in a one-sided deal. We shall keep it in storage. We shall keep it available. The farmers will have the cost of storing it on the farms; the national treasury will have the cost of storing another part of it under the storage program. China may or may not buy, but we shall keep it available.
This is the most one-sided agreement I have ever seen. I have been making inquiries, and I am confident that China has not agreed in a firm manner to buy a single bushel of
Supply-Trade and Commerce wheat beyond the 28 million bushels to be delivered between June 1 and November 30. We have agreed that if China wants the wheat we shall have it. We may have it, all right.

speechtext: I should like to ask the hon. member whether he is against this deal that we have completed with China.

I have made my position clear. I am against this thing being blown up as a firm agreement when it is no such thing. I am against false publicity, and I am against the farmers of western Canada being shown what could turn out to be a hoax unless the Minister of Trade and Commerce-and he is the minister who can do it-assures us that communist China will buy this quantity of grain and that Canada is prepared to sell it no matter what price communist China may offer and will pay. I am suggesting that this is just another of those areas where this government is operating by hiring public relations people to put something in the best possible light from the standpoint of the government, but not necessarily very close to the hard facts and the substance of what is involved.
Let us be perfectly clear about this. This is no firm transaction for the sale of 186 million bushels of wheat. This is just what it is not. This is a firm transaction for 28 million bushels of wheat. Beyond that China commits herself to nothing. The Canadian government says it has a storage plan under which we shall have the balance of 158 million bushels available if China should decide to buy it on the basis of future contracts, when both price and quantity will be under negotiation.

Now that the hon. member for Assiniboia has completed his comments I believe the committee will not mind if I take this opportunity, the first I have, to congratulate the new Minister of Trade and Commerce.
(Translation):
Mr. Chairman, I have always admired the former minister of transport. I hope you will not mind if I take this opportunity to congratulate him although the minister is a veteran of the cabinet on his appointment as Minister of Trade and Commerce.
In the last few months, it has been repeatedly said that the province of Quebec is on the go. If the province of Quebec is on the go and if the rest of the country is on the go, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees) can claim part of the credit for it, because it is due to his efforts and his marvellous talent for organization.
Instead of indulging in pointless and groundless criticism of the type we have just

Supply-Trade and Commerce heard a lew moments ago from the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), I shall just take a few seconds of the time of the house to place before the Minister of Trade and Commerce a suggestion which has repeatedly been made to me by experts in commission sales.
It has been suggested to me repeatedly by experienced salesmen that I ask the government to try hiring people to sell on a commission basis on behalf of Canada in our trade commissioner service abroad. I think such a move would produce practical results, because there would be an incentive for such agents to sell more.
I know things are not done that way under the present system, but perhaps amendments might be made to the legal foundations of the department before hiring such salesmen to represent Canada abroad, whether they be paid on a commission basis by the companies doing the business, or by the government.
In any event, even if it required amendments to the Civil Service Act and to the government's hiring practices, I think it would yield practical results.
I therefore place this suggestion before the minister, and I leave it to the Department of Trade and Commerce to organize such a system and put it into operation. I do think the idea has merit and that it should gain acceptance or at least be thoroughly examined by the Department of Trade and Commerce.

I have a few brief remarks which I intend to make at this time. It is a mere platitude to say how important trade is to our country, both externally and internally. We have been listening to comments on one important incident of trade. Another aspect we should not overlook is not merely material aspect but the extent to which it indicates that interdependence which, I suppose, is the best hope we have of peace. We ought to welcome it in every way and in every place we can find it.
I suppose when we look back to the nineteenth century it is clear that the peacefulness which, in the main, characterized that century was largely due to the influence of Britain and, most of all, to Britain's free trade policy, which one might say spanned the world and did so much to make people live happily together. Since then we have had a half century which in some ways seems almost like a mad period. We have encountered difficulties in the sphere of trade and elsewhere which call for new qualities, qualities which perhaps we have never had to show before except in time of war.

I should like to read a sentence or two from that great public servant, as I regard him, Adlai Stevenson, who seems not only to think clearly about these matters but to have a wonderful gift for expressing himself:
What lies ahead of us in this bewildering century is invisible but it may be even more significant. In the past the north Atlantic nations dominated the world. But they could not control themselves, and after their great world wars the power and influence of Europe declined; Russia and the United States suddenly emerged as the two dominant powers. Already the brief day of two power domination is passing and new centres of power are rising from old ashes in Asia.
Let me repeat these important words:
-new centres of power are rising from old ashes in Asia.
This is something we should all be taking most seriously. He goes on to say:
By the end of the century China and India will be industrialized, and China's population will be close to a billion.
Then he says:
To guide us through these uncharted seas, to comprehend and direct prodigious forces now shaping the new world, is going to make heavy demands on our resources of wisdom, leadership, self-discipline and magnanimity.
Let me call your attention again to these words:
-wisdom, leadership, self-discipline and magnanimity.
Let me now come closer home and use words which should come directly to the mind of each of us, because they come from a man of ability in private industry who has been drafted into public service in an important capacity. I refer to Mr. George de Young, chairman of the productivity council. He used words which I found a bit startling but which no one should disregard. He said:
Passive confidence-
Note the word "passive".
Passive confidence in our now disproved technological and economical superiority, and continued factional and segmental rivalry have resulted in Canada's economy no longer being able to provide work for all its own people through private enterprise.
Mr. de Young has been on a mission to the European economic community, and he has the following to say about that:
The mission concluded that government, business and labour in Canada must immediately adjust to this vital new economic area, check rising costs here, and achieve maximum utilization of resources, skills and manpower.
Our own Minister of Trade and Commerce has been speaking plainly to us about this. He used an illustration in regard to our own performance here which I found interesting, coming from him. He said we had gone soft, and compared us to a boxer who had gone soft. The Minister of Trade and Commerce

was once a boxer himself and I would rather he boxed with other individuals than me, because in his day he was a formidable individual at a strange place called Cambridge. The minister has talked plainly when he has spoken and has not pulled any punches in telling us what we need to do.
The same can be said of his deputy, who was speaking the other day in Montreal when he used words which I wish to read. He said this:
-problems and challenges in the economic and trade field, which stand in the doorway to our future. We must be concerned with these challenges today, for the future is tomorrow, and it is in the future that we, and our children, will be spending the rest of our lives.
Then he had this to say:
I am sure none of you are under any illusions about the difficulties and frustrations which face us. The economies of western Europe and Asia have been rebuilt.
I repeat the word "rebuilt". He went on to say:
We are confronted with bitter competition from many countries equally as hungry as we are, for a bigger share of world markets. Goods from the United Kingdom, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Japan, for example, are competing with our own in foreign markets and even in our own back yard. These goods, produced in new factories equipped with the most modern machinery and by highly skilled workers, whose wage rates are lower than those in Canada, are of excellent quality and design. In many cases they are lower in price.
The Department of Trade and Commerce has done much. I believe that the conference held here late last autumn accomplished a great deal, first of all in stimulating and encouraging our own trade commissioners and, second, by stimulating and directing the efforts of our exporters. The problem of unemployment is still serious, but there is no mystery about it; none whatever. We had a boom; some people say it began in 1935 and some say it began in 1940, but at any rate it lasted until after the middle of the 1950's. Then it flattened out a bit, but it has not turned into a depression. We are still doing well, as was reported in the Winnipeg Free Press some months ago. That article referred to a curious situation where we had substantial unemployment in the midst of prosperity.
This is a strange new phenomenon. I think the reasons for it are perfectly clear. At the time the boom flattened out a bit, competition from abroad increased enormously. Western European nations, as we know, were given a flying start, which really gave business a fresh start under the Marshall plan. The workmen there realized that their own hard work would produce benefit for themselves, and I think perhaps they have that sense more strongly than we in this country have.
Supply-Trade and Commerce At the same time other things happened, such as automation. Further, many individuals were leaving farms because one man on a farm could grow many times that which could be grown before. We had all these influences occurring at the same time.
I think everyone will agree that at the present time what we need more than anything else is increased world trade. I was very interested in speaking with an acute observer a few weeks ago who made an interesting remark about our own country, looking back over 60 years. He pointed out that in the early years of this century our economy was sparked by a railway boom. After that we had the motor car industry boom, which this man described as being now in what he called a state of high level stagnation. He next pointed out that we then had the chemical industry boom, followed by an electronic industry boom and, one might add, the boom resulting from two wars. This man went on to say that he thought the next economic impulse in our country must come from raising economic conditions in underdeveloped countries.
This is the subject I want to speak about now. I have done so before, and as long as Mr. Speaker will allow me and while there is breath in me I will continue to do so, because I believe this is the most important thing which faces us now. I think we are not alive to it. I do not flatter myself that my words are going to change the minds of the people, but I should hope that the press would take more interest in it. A few of the better newspapers have done so already, but I think this subject should appear in every newspaper. However, this is just my own opinion.
I would like to refer now to the experience we had 15 years ago, in 1946, when we made a loan of $1,250 million to Great Britain. I would like to refer to what was said at that time by the then minister in his speech introducing this subject. He said that this loan would be just as much in our own interests as in the interests of the people to whom it was being made. As a matter of fact, that advance to the people of Britain in 1946 was followed by the purchase of hundreds of millions of dollars of our exports and was of great assistance to us in those years after the war.
I would like to make a point now that I have made here before, because it seems to me to illustrate the trade advantage derived from this kind of thing. That is, trade is aid, or aid is trade, whichever way you like to put it. Some years ago when we made a gift -I am not talking about gifts now but about loans-under the Colombo plan of some $35

Supply-Trade and Commerce million, 95 per cent was in the form of manufactured goods, which represented Canadian employment. We did not ship barrels of dollars over to India.
We now have a new impulse from President Kennedy. His views may not rank quite as high today as they did a month ago, but after all, any man can make a mistake and recover from it. Anyone who has read his statement to congress will agree that it was a great document indeed and showed a constructive attitude. One of the great things he did was to point out that if aid to those countries is going to be effective it must be done not year by year but based on several years-he suggested five-so it can be used in a planned way.
Then I come to that great paper we all respect, the London Economist. It is a very conservative paper, and I mean conservative with a small "c". I think it is full of realism and experience. I was very interested in what it had to say about assistance. It made one or two very practical suggestions. It referred to the meeting of the development assistance group which took place in London about a month ago. This is what it said:
What the Americans would like each of their allies to do is to commit itself to give definite amounts of assistance, and to co-ordinate individual national programs in some international new deal designed to capture the imagination of the world.
That, of course, is what is necessary. Next, the Economist speaks of the dramatic effect which would be caused if a lead were given in Europe. Then it adds this:
Now, in short, is the historic opportunity for Mr. Macmillan to make a speech that could launch a whole new conception of international economic relations, and for people here to start thinking about the best form that a world aid scheme could take.
I have no time to deal with the details of what the Economist said, but I want to draw attention to one thing which I think is very practical. What they have in mind is a loan for five years at a time. They point out that the contributions would not have to be made from tax appropriations immediately. They say:
The strain that these contributions would impose would then fall upon the contributing countries only as they were used-mainly-
And note this:
-mainly in order to buy their capital equipment or the services of some of their technicians.
In other words the loan would be spent at home. Then the Economist remarks shrewdly enough:
This "strain" would thus show itself at first in the form of a recorded increase in the donor country's export surplus, which is not the sort of strain that usually causes great difficulties.


They are saying the same thing that I said a moment ago about our Colombo plan contribution, namely that it represented Canadian employment. The Economist also suggests that the international monetary fund could assist in the problem of foreign exchange which will arise. I hope to go into that matter again later this session, indeed to bring it up again when I have the chance, but I quote the Economist as a witness of proven experience, of common sense and realism. Its comments should indicate that this is not pie in the sky but is common sense and good business.
I have already referred the committee to our own experience in 1946 when the minister of finance, in speaking on this billion and a quarter dollar credit, said:
The need for a credit of this magnitude and on these terms springs not only from the effects of the war upon Britain, but also from the vital importance to Canada of the re-establishment, expansion and continued development of foreign trade.
That is what we did in 1946. It succeeded then and there is no reason why it cannot succeed today.
I am not going to take up too much of the time of the committee, but I do want to refer to the great world figures who have studied this matter, who are giving their lives to it and whose opinions I believe are more valuable than any other opinions we can get. I refer to Hoffman, Black and Adlai Stevenson. I prescribe for hon. members a course of reading of some of the things they have written. Until we have read what they have to say I suggest we are not in any position to make up our minds. I have a pamphlet by Adlai Stevenson which I think is one of the most important bits of reading I have done. I am going to see whether I can get our mechanical staff to make some copies, and if I can I am going to take the liberty of putting them in the post office boxes of hon. members.
Again, without giving figures, I want to remind the committee of what I said before. Paul Hoffman gives astronomical figures as to what will be done in the way of foreign trade if we raise the buying power of the underdeveloped countries, those hundreds of millions of people who go to bed hungry every night. Do not let us forget that if we raised their purchasing power, that is the per capita income, by even a dollar a year over the next 10 years the results would be astronomical.
I should like to refer to another matter with which I was greatly struck in reading the Prime Minister's speech at the United Nations last September, a speech which caused such world-wide interest. At that

time he had a good deal to say about the new states coming into existence. He said:
Since the war 14 colonies and territories comprising half a billion people have achieved complete freedom within the commonwealth.
I learned also that France had also given independence to 14 colonies. But this political independence is going to be a barren and negative thing unless economic independence goes with it. We have this whole flock of new countries which are now aware of their miserable conditions. I noticed the other day that a far eastern statesman was in the United States. He was talking to the big producers of radio and television in Hollywood. He accused them of being revolutionaries, because he said that for the first time these producers in Hollywood had made clear to the people of the underdeveloped countries the terrible plight they were in, although it is hard to believe it is true that they had not realized it before.
I think it is fair to consider the urgent need from the point of view of the underdeveloped countries in the commonwealth. I talked about India before. I shall not take the time of the committee now, but I do want to say this. Serious, competent people who have come back from India after months of study have said that she is entitled to assistance on economic grounds. Some of them are bankers. Three, including Sir Oliver Franks, head of one of the big British banks, representing leading world banks, came back from India and said she was entitled to assistance. Others have done so as well, including those 1 have mentioned.
I am not going to take more time. I make no apologies for bringing this up again. I believe it is something that we should all be interested in. I believe it to be in our own interest, just as it proved to be in 1946. Plans made then paid off abundantly. For that reason I put it in this way. I am not able to believe, and I do not find men whose opinions I value most saying, that there are any clear indications that we shall be able to deal with the problem of unemployment unless by a substantial increase in the mass of world trade. I find scarcely anyone who disagrees with this. Also, what I read from the deputy minister makes it very clear that the difficult competition we face from the western European nations makes our problem that much greater. The minister made this clear also. The western European nations have come back in a big way with what I call a flying start. Of course people are entitled to reach their own conclusions, but the stock market at the present time seems to believe that things are on the uptrend; it has a hunch that everything is going to be all right. People are busy climbing on the
Supply-Trade and Commerce bandwagon. This seems to me to indicate there is every reason to believe that it is in our own interest-I do not think the minister will disagree with this for a minute; indeed, I am sure he has said it-to insist on an increase in world trade.
I pause on the moral argument. If we had those miserable people living within our sight we could not stand it, of course. Being compassionate people we would act on that basis. I am not going to deal with that today, or with the political side.
Of course from the political side we should be deeply concerned. We should be deeply concerned about helping these people so that they can work out their economic salvation by the institutions of freedom and not by the institutions of totalitarianism.
One only needs to pause a moment to realize how much that means to us. I have quoted before in the house from the book by Chester Bowles, one-time ambassador to India, his reference to a conversation he had with an Indian statesman who said to him, "You people, whether or not you like it, are in competition with the communists. First of all, you are in competition because we are going to ask whether you are making more rapid economic progress than they are. Second, you are in competition because we are going to compare the help we get from them with the help we get from you." We cannot overlook that for one moment. The same man said to Bowles, "Of course, if India goes the whole of southeast Asia goes".
I leave this with the house and I ask hon. members to consider it. I shall try to place the speech by Stevenson in hon. members' hands, and I would beg hon. members to read it. I do not believe anyone who reads it will fail to be impressed with the urgency and the importance of reaching the right decision on this question.

Mr. Chairman, I have been very much moved by the remarks we have just listened to by the hon. member for Greenwood in what was a truly Liberal speech. I would remind the hon. gentleman that in times past he has talked about strengthening the opposition in the house, and I assure him that if he feels he can contribute to the strengthening of the opposition there is always a light in the window for him on this side of the house.
Indeed, it might be a very useful thing for the hon. member to be associated with those who originated the policies he commended so highly today. I thank him for his commendation of the courageous things that were done by Mr. Mackenzie King, Mr. Ilsley and Mr. St. Laurent in 1946, because it did take courage at that time. The loan to Britain and

Supply-Trade and Commerce the other loans that were made at that time were not made with the unanimous approval of everyone in the country. It was a policy that required courage and fortitude, a policy that was attacked in certain parts of this country, particularly, I regret to have to recall, by the friends of the hon. gentleman in one part of the country under the slogan, "Les Liberaux donnent aux etrangers, Duples-sis donne a sa province".
Notwithstanding that kind of appeal, the majority of the Canadian people in every province approved this policy. We have been able to build on it and I think Canada, under whichever government has been in office, has no reason to apologize for what has been done in this field of aid for underdeveloped countries. I think we have given a lead both in measures for the restoration of trade and in the inauguration and building up of the Colombo plan; and, because of the high respect in which the hon. gentleman is held not merely in this house but in many parts of the country, I sincerely trust his remarks will fall on listening ears and not on deaf ears.

speechtext: If I may have one moment, Mr. Chairman, I wish, of course, to repudiate the suggestion of the hon. gentleman that whenever one says anything that he considers sensible it is a Liberal remark. I should like to thank the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville and the hon. member for Greenwood for the very constructive remarks they have made this morning. I should also like to comment briefly on the remarks of the hon. member for Assiniboia. In doing so I should like to quote a paragraph from the statement of the Minister of Agriculture when he spoke in the house a day or two ago about the wheat agreement with China. As found on page 4205 of Hansard he said:
I have made it clear that there is a long term agreement. Under that agreement one contract has been signed. Each future contract will be negotiated in respect to price and quantity.
In speaking this morning the hon. member for Assiniboia, it seemed to me, tried to make out that the Minister of Agriculture had in some way misled the house as to what amount was in this agreement. I think it is evident

from my quotation of the minister's words that he made it very clear exactly what this agreement is. On behalf of the government may I say that we believe this agreement is a good agreement, one which will benefit greatly our wheat and grain farmers and the Canadian economy as a whole. From the words of the hon. member for Assiniboia it is quite clear that if he and his party were the government of Canada today they would not have signed this agreement, with its great benefits to the farmers of Canada and to the Canadian economy as a whole.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am exceedingly disappointed by the statement of the minister, because it confirms in a very real way all the suspicions I have had about the agreement. No one has complained about the government signing an agreement. I am not even complaining about the signing of this agreement, although I have not seen it and think it should be produced. I am complaining, however, about the very misleading terms in which the minister referred to this agreement.
This is the history of sales to China this year. On February 2 there was an announcement by the government of the sale of 40 million bushels of wheat and barley valued at $60 million. On May 2 the minister announced in the house that in addition to this earlier sale there had been a sale of 2.2 million bushels of wheat valued at $3.7 million. The next sale the government announced was the sale of 28 million bushels of wheat and 17 million bushels of barley with an estimated total value of $66 million. Under the long term agreement the terms of payment are 25 per cent cash and the balance in 270 days.
But in order to get this additional agreement for the period June 1 to November 30 -and the minister can correct me if he believes I am wrong-Canada has had to do a great many things. The government has agreed to provide, and parliament will have to provide, a $50 million credit in order that this transaction may be undertaken. So that what the minister should have announced when he came back was not a gigantic sale of $362 million worth of grain, which has not taken place and for which an agreement has not been signed, although he talked about a sale, but rather a second agreement for a certain quantity of grain. At the same time he should have announced that in order to have this firm agreement signed for a much smaller sum, Canada has had to provide a credit of $50 million.
The Minister of Agriculture has talked about a sale of this order, namely 186.7 million bushels of wheat and 46.7 million bushels of barley worth approximately $362 million. He has told us the value and has

called it a sale, but there is no sale. If there is to be any sale in the future, the price and the quantity will be negotiated. The farmers of the prairies have been fooled into believing, and have been kidded, that this is a sale of 186.7 million bushels of wheat [DOT]-they have even got it to the decimal point -and 46.7 million bushels of barley, which is worth $362 million. The only people who have decided to make a firm commitment are the people of Canada. No firm commitment has been made by China.
My understanding is that when a sale is made it must be a contract entered into by two persons. They agree to specific things. In this case the two parties would be the wheat board and the China Resources Company. No such transaction has been agreed upon. There is no firm agreement beyond November 30 this year, and I put that to the minister. China has committed itself to absolutely nothing. Our Minister of Agriculture called it a sale of this order which was worth $362 million. He pointed out what this would do for the country. I ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce to deny what I have said. I know he cannot.

This subject of the wheat agreement certainly has generated a great deal of heat. Undoubtedly the agreement is of major importance. I must say that the allegations made by the leader of the group on my right, the C.C.F. group, are of a very serious nature. If they are sustained when

Supply-Trade and Commerce the agreement is produced, they will certainly represent a matter of major importance to the country.
I listened with great interest to the announcement of the Minister of Agriculture in common with all other hon. members in the house. I attached great importance to it and subsequently I read the statement very carefully. When I read it carefully there were some questions about it that concerned me. I did not want to put the questions to the Minister of Trade and Commerce yesterday because, as I mentioned in my remarks, he has a truncated department. When I made that reference I had in mind the fact that the wheat board had been taken from his jurisdiction and given to the Minister of Agriculture, rightly or wrongly. I thought the questions that arose in my mind about this contract were ones that should properly concern the other department. I had some questions, however, concerning the form of payment as they related to trade generally. The agreement itself, as announced, did raise questions in my mind, so I took what I thought was the proper course and put a motion on the order paper requesting production of the document.
This is something that cannot be debated in the committee at this stage. I would expect that the document would be produced, and we could then see whether or not the things that have been said about the agreement are right. They may or may not be. I simply do not know. I felt that the course adopted ought to be explained to the committee in case hon. members should assume from the failure to deal with it in my remarks yesterday that we somehow thought the agreement was not of major importance to the economy of this country, or of any significance to agriculture. It was simply a matter of taking the view that the agreement itself was something that came under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Agriculture.
I should have liked to ask this Minister of Trade and Commerce some questions about it, and indeed raise some arguments with him about it, but I thought it improper to do so. I should like the minister's view on what the situation is with respect to jurisdiction over this subject of the sale of wheat, now that jurisdiction over the wheat board and the board of grain commissioners has been taken from the Minister of Trade and Commerce and given to the Minister of Agriculture.

As I understand it, the criticisms made by the hon. member for Assiniboia are derived from his having read the statement made by the minister to the House of Commons. As I listened to the minister the other day it seemed perfectly clear to me. It was perfectly clear that there was no misleading of the house in that statement. That was my feeling when I listened to the statement.
If I am wrong, I want to be corrected, but I understood the hon. member's criticism was of statements which appeared in the press, and that when he saw the actual Hansard record he realized that those statements were a little too enthusiastic. Sometimes newspapers do become enthusiastic, but the idea that the minister should be blamed or was in any way responsible for misleading the public is, I think, something which is utterly unfair and which I hope the hon. member will withdraw.

Mr. Chairman, we are really getting the runaround. The minister now says there is an agreement. Nobody has been denying that there is an agreement, or that there is some document which has been signed. I should like to see the agreement. Certainly there is an agreement, but it is the most lopsided agreement I have ever heard of, where Canada agrees to provide and keep available this quantity of grain and, as far as I can tell, China has committed herself to nothing. To support his contention that there is some commitment the minister reads from his colleague's statement the words:
I have made It clear that there is a long term agreement.
Of course there is, but it does not necessarily mean a thing. China does not commit herself to take a quantity of grain. She does not commit herself to the price that will be paid. Everything will be under negotiation except the Canadian part, which provides that we shall keep the grain available. Countries such as India have wanted our grain in the past and have gone into the markets of the world to obtain 586 million bushels of wheat in a four year period. We should have been engaged, long before, in the sale of our grain in the distressed areas of the world. However, the agreements we make

should be agreements which provide for the sale of certain quantities of grain under guaranteed arrangements, and when agreements are signed they should mean something. I suggest that this agreement in its present terms does not say anything at all in support of the impressions which the minister sought to convey.

Before the vote carries I wish to raise another matter in connection with the administration of the department, having to do with the advice available to the minister from economists and related officials of the department.
It will be recalled that in January of 1958 a well known episode took place in the House of Commons, when the present Prime Minister made reference to a document called "The Canadian Economic Outlook, 1957". There was considerable controversy at the time with regard to this. It was a document marked "secret" on some pages and "confidential" on others, a document from which most of the blue covers had been torn off. When it was tabled a small part of them remained.
In any event, the document was an analysis prepared by economists in the department on a confidential basis for use by the government in helping them to formulate policy. Subsequent examination of the document showed that the Prime Minister in referring to it in the course of his speech had taken excerpts from it which were completely out of context. Study of the document after it had been tabled also showed that it was a comprehensive one, a document of a type which would be very helpful to the government in formulating policy by way of legislation or otherwise.
The next year, after a lot of delay and a lot of argument in the house, "The Canadian Economic Outlook, 1958" was tabled. A great deal of argument took place about it, but finally it was tabled and it appeared to be a document of the same general nature as previously. Then in 1960 when a motion was put forward asking for the tabling of "The Canadian Economic Outlook, 1959", the document was not produced; in fact there was a refusal to produce it. The motion was voted on by the house and the government succeeded in voting down the request for the production of that document without giving any reason at all for this action, though the government itself had set the precedent for the tabling of the document.
Later, when we raised the matter on the estimates of the department last year, after a great deal of somewhat heated argument the minister of trade and commerce of that day, now the Minister of Veterans Affairs, took the position that there was no such

document as "The Canadian Economic Outlook, 1959". Be that as it may, there appeared to be a contradiction at that time between the position taken when the production of the document was sought and the statement made when the matter was raised again on the estimates, when the minister said no such document had been prepared.
The question I wish to ask the present minister is this. Does he have such a document prepared for the use of the government? That is the narrow question I want to ask.

I am sure he is thoroughly familiar with the difficulties there have been during recent years with respect to the exchange problem in Brazil. The result is that in the past year, particularly, there has been a growing accumulation of salt fish for which apparently there is no immediate market.

Mr. Chairman, I rose rather unexpectedly just before one o'clock; I had not realized that we seemed to be so near the conclusion of debate on the minister's first item, perhaps because I was unfortunately not able to be here yesterday. Instead of putting the position in my own words I think, if the committee will bear with me for a moment, I will put it in the words of Mr. Harold Shea as they appeared in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald, of March 16, 1961. Mr. Shea had obviously done a good deal of hard work on this problem. I think he has set out the position in a more succinct way than I could do it just by speaking off the cuff which, as hon. members know, I sometimes do. The article is headed:
And now a salt fish crisis for Maritimes.
With a growing cod surplus at home and a mounting dollar shortage in traditional markets, exporters have called upon Ottawa for assistance through give-aways to Congo or long term credits for foreign countries.
The dispatch itself reads:
Problems of currency and competition are creating severe marketing difficulties for salt fish exporters in the Atlantic provinces and, unless the above average stockpile can be sold soon, lower returns to fishermen may be expected this year.
This situation is causing concern to the federal government, too.
I hope Mr. Shea was right in this. I continue:
It has been asked to help, but officials candidly admit that there does not appear to be any easy solution.
Well, I do not think there is an easy solution. That is why we have governments. If all our problems could be solved easily I imagine we would dispense with government altogether, especially in the economic field. The dispatch goes on:
At a time when exporters on the east coast would normally be clearing away the last stocks of
Supply-Trade and Commerce salted cod and shipping them off to the traditional markets in the Caribbean, there is a heavy holdover of this fish with little hope of volume sales.
And with a new salt fishing season only weeks away-
Unfortunately it is not getting on very fast yet because of the ice, as the minister knows. If he does not, if he would consult the officials of his former department-transport-he would soon find out. I continue:
And with a new salt fishing season only weeks away, the stockpiles are going to grow and grow unless a way is found around marketing difficulties.
As of January 31, according to government figures, the salt fish exporters in the maritimes were carrying 443,000 cases of salted cod (100 pounds to the case). At the same time last year, the reserve supply was less than half that.
Sale prospects between now and the start of the new season are not bright. Orders are held for only 180,000 eases, which would leave the shippers with a backlog of 263,000 cases. What has caused this marketing problem?
I think it is worth putting these things on record because perhaps the minister can bring us more up to date than Mr. Shea has done about these particular markets.
Brazil, with a new government, hasn't yet decided how many dollars it will release for salt fish.
Spain, normally an importing country, is now selling fish to Puerto Rico and Portugal, two of Canada's customers.
Notwithstanding that statement, sir, I imagine that if we were producing the right kind of fish we could still sell fish to Spain, because I do not think the Spaniards can catch and cure the kind of fish they want for the high priced Spanish market. This is a problem on which I intend to say something when the estimates of the Department of Fisheries are in committee, but it would not be entirely fair to take up the time of the committee on the minister's estimates. The article goes on:
Cuba, suffering a dollar shortage because of the drastic cut in American tourist travel to the island, has run out of money. It has ceased buying fish from Canada and Norway, and proposes to offer, instead of money, such items as fruits, vegetables, tobacco, rum and sisal in exchange for fish.
Jamaica, Puerto Rico, British Guiana and the Dominican Republic are heavily overstocked with salted fish, and are not in the market immediately.
Dominican Republic is apparently short of dollars too, because there have been reports that accounts with maritime companies are several months in arrears.
With stocks 50 per cent heavier than last year, and with such dismal marketing prospects, and with a new fishing season scheduled to open soon, maritime exporters, and fishermen, are in trouble.
They have appealed to the government for assistance.

Mr. Chairman, this morning's discussion concerning the sale of grain to red China took an extraordinary turn.
I followed it with great interest. The government and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees) were clearly on the defensive.
I have read a number of times the statement made on May 2 by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton), and I noted particularly a paragraph on page 4205 of Hansard in which the minister said:
A sale of this order will spread substantial benefits through the Canadian economy.
In the same statement, the minister had previously announced a deal of some $362 million.
That is what the Minister of Agriculture said, that is what we understood and what Canadian newspapers and the Canadian people understood.
But there is more. In this morning's Gazette, we find the following statement made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green):
(Text):
External Affairs Minister Green said yesterday that the big Canadian grain sale to communist China might be one of the many factors taken into consideration in the recognition of red China in the United Nations.
(Translation):
The government very definitely gave us the impression that this grain deal with communist China was worth $362 million.
If we go carefully over the details supplied by the Minister of Agriculture in the statement he made on Tuesday, May 2, we note the following facts.
First of all, the minister referred to the sale of 40 million bushels of wheat and barley, valued at approximately $60 million contracted between the Canadian wheat board and the China Resources Company. That is the first sale, a bilateral contract between China and Canada.


Second, the minister informed us that there is an additional sale to China of 2.2 million bushels of wheat, valued at $3.7 million, for shipment during March to May 1961. This is also a sale that puts China, as well as Canada, under certain bilateral obligations.
The minister then made another statement about a $66 million contract, signed under a long term agreement, by which China and Canada have mutually committed themselves, the latter to deliver goods, the former to pay an agreed price.
I therefore submit that there are three contracts, duly signed, and imposing a legal obligation upon China and Canada.
As for the rest of his statement, I suggest we have again been victims of a new vision. In fact, this agreement for $362 million worth of wheat and barley is only a promise to buy on the part of China. It is therefore on the part of Canada a unilateral commitment under which it would undertake to keep available for China 186.7 million bushels of wheat and 46.7 million bushels of barley from the 1st of June, 1961 to December 1963. Moreover, China would not be bound to buy the above mentioned quantities during this period.
Therefore for China this would amount to no more than an insurance policy covering the period from June 1961 to December 1963, in case its future crops fail to fill the gap that might exist in this year's wheat and barley crops.
What impressed me most this morning is that the matter was pointed out to the Minister of Trade and Commerce with a request that he then give an explanation concerning this agreement. Well, the minister found nothing better to do than read again parts of the statement made to last May 2 by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton). Unquestionably, these are disturbing facts we are now facing and not only are we entitled to an explanation but we also have the right to ask that any agreement signed by this government and the government of China, or a Chinese wheat committee, be tabled immediately, so that we may know whether we have not been left under a false impression following the statement made by the Minister of Agriculture on May 2.
Mr. Chairman, it would be proper at this stage, while we are on the subject of agreements, to review the fundamentals of any sales contract.
What is a sales contract? Let me refer to the civil code of the province of Quebec, section 1472, which reads as follows:
A sale is a contract whereby a person gives something to another person for a price in money which the latter undertakes to pay.

Mr. Chairman, first, it is essential for me to know the facts. In the Ottawa Journal of May 3, may be read the following statement made by the Minister of Agriculture, following a question put to him by Richard Jackson, a newspaperman.
(Text):
But wasn't trade a two-way street, and didn't the Chinese hope to recover some of their $326 million through sales of their own to Canada?
Could be, agreed Mr. Hamilton.
(Translation):
Well, Mr. Chairman, after all this window dressing about a sale which, in the main, is nothing of the kind, I think we are entitled to some explanations. In my opinion, it is quite obvious, in the light of the facts now given us, that the government of China has contracted no legal obligation in regard to the greater amount of money concerned for the purchase of that wheat. If we re-read the statement made by the Minister of Agriculture, the only conclusion we arrive at is that both the public and parliament were left under a false impression, an impression that even the figures provided by the minister fail to support. Therefore, I think we are entitled to demand the tabling of all documents and agreements concluded and signed, that we may know the actual scope of the sales made; in other words, in order that we may have the whole truth.

The contention is made, and I repeat it now, that this program, in so far as it concerns the relocation of industry or encouraging industry to stay where it is already, will not bring forward one single case.
The minister has a responsibility in connection with this matter. He has not properly outlined exactly what his role in this program is to be. It is part of the government's method of trying to create the impression that it is doing something to meet this serious problem of unemployment.
The Minister of Labour, when he presents his estimates, will be called on to report his achievements with regard to this program, as will the Minister of Finance. We are now dealing with the Department of Trade and Commerce, and we should have from the minister some indication of the number of applications which have been received, together with an indication of what this is going to mean in keeping down the numbers of unemployed and preventing a recurrence of unemployment.

What we shall want from the minister is a report which will indicate that this program has substance and is not merely a facade. The minister has been very active in meeting with his trade commissioners. He has been very active, he tells us, in meeting with the industrialists of this country, although I see he has begun to scold the industrialists for failing, he says, to follow the directions he has given.
In any event, the Minister of Labour is not alone responsible for doing something about unemployment. That is a responsibility which must be shared by all members of the government, notably by those responsible for the Department of Trade and Commerce, the Department of Finance, the Department of Defence Production, the Department of National Defence, the Department of National Health and Welfare and others. This is a responsibility which does not belong only to the little Minister of Labour. It is one which also devolves on the shoulders of the big Minister of Trade and Commerce. I think we are entitled to hear from the minister some indication of what the program means in practical results.
The hon. gentleman has changed his understanding as to the responsibility of the government toward unemployment. Only two or three months ago he said this was a problem which was now outside the scope of government responsibility, that it was something which was the responsibility of all the people of Canada. This is not, of course, what the Minister of Trade and Commerce said when he spoke on this subject when in opposition as a private member. Nor is it what he said


as one of the chief tune makers of the administration during the elections of 1957 and 1958. The minister cannot hope to satisfy members of this committee merely by his friendly manner, his engaging smile and the fine impression we gather when we look at him. Fine impressions of this sort are not sufficient to warrant a conclusion that the minister is fully discharging his responsibility.
I should like to hear from the Minister of Trade and Commerce today what his solution is to the problem of unemployment. He has a responsibility in this matter. The Prime Minister made a most amazing statement when he said that the Bladen royal commission was not one which concerned the Department of Trade and Commerce but was of primary concern to the Department of Finance. I do not know whether this means that the government intends to take some fiscal steps at long last. I do not know whether this foreshadows the abolition of the excise tax on automobiles. I hope it means that, and I hope it means other things as well. But I cannot conceive that the Minister of Trade and Commerce would concur in the view stated by the Prime Minister that his department is not vitally concerned with whatever recommendations are made by Professor Bladen with regard to an industry which means so much to Canada.
I have not in the past pursued the Minister of Trade and Commerce on his estimates, but I do pursue him today in respect of this matter because I want some indication, and I believe this committee and the whole country want some indication, of how this program of double depreciation is developing and what it is doing to meet the objective set for it. speechtext:
I was trying to help the minister to indicate that it went further than that. If he will look at the order in council he will find that it applies as well to a plant already in existence in a distressed area and in respect of the production of goods in that plant in that distressed area. But the point is that the program is not going to be of any value whatsoever because this is a program designed to be operative for one year only. Surely it cannot possibly achieve anything approaching a substantial solution to the problem of unemployment or the mitigation of it.
We have had an amazing revelation today from the minister as to the number of applications in respect of those applications that come under his jurisdiction. He has, in addition, given us the number of areas that have made application for the program under the Minister of Labour. But the statistics clearly show how bankrupt this program is. It is inconceivable that a government, faced with the problem of unemployment we have in this country at the present time, should seek to try to put over the house and the people of Canada the impression that this is a program that is really seriously designed to deal with unemployment. I doubt whether any government in Canadian history has ever brought forward a program which on the slightest examination has been revealed to be so inadequate and so unworthy of presentation in this house.

I say to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that if he alone had the responsibility for this matter I am sure, whatever might have been the weaknesses in the thinking processes that might have accompanied the idea, the program would at least have had much greater substance than this. For the government to think that it can put over the house, the businessmen of the nation and the unemployed of the country the idea that this program designed for one year is capable of doing the job is a simply monstrous suggestion. It is part of the pattern of behaviour of the government from the beginning of this session.
The government will be able to say, "See what we have done. We have brought forward a program of double depreciation. We have brought forward a program to provide for vocational rehabilitation". In fact all the government has done has been to bring forward in a new form an idea and program that have been in existence in this country for 12 years. "See what we have done," the government will say. "We have brought forward the productivity council". But at the same time hon. members opposite do not tell the unsuspecting public that this program is to be effective only in the long range future. "See what we have done," hon. gentlemen opposite will say, "We have brought forward legislation to assist small business," when in fact all they have done has been to bring forward legislation to assist in the improvement of the premises of certain business categories.
I say to the Minister of Trade and Commerce this program is not an effective one. This program in principle could be an effective one but it would have to be a program that would give relief by way of accelerated depreciation for an extended period. Why does the minister not do what has been done in England? Why does he not do what has been done in Belgium and in West Germany? In the case of these countries the lowest period prevailing under such programs is, I believe, eight years.
If we had a program that was going to be in existence for a period of eight years there would be some inducement for a company to move from Toronto to Essex county or from Ottawa to Cornwall where there is a serious unemployment problem. In Cornwall over 16 per cent of the work force is out of work. But what company is going to move from Ottawa to Cornwall when all it is going to get is the benefit of this principle of double depreciation for one year?
I say to the government members that they do not like it when we criticize them for not doing anything about unemployment. They characterize our efforts as being those of men 90205-6-275
Supply-Trade and Commerce who are simply bent on presenting the gloomiest picture and delighting in it. Well, that is an argument but it is not a fair argument; it is not an honourable argument. Today we are face to face with an examination of the government program, a program that was vaunted by the Minister of Finance in the baby budget. The word went out throughout the country that the government at long last had recognized the urgency of the problem and was going to do something along the lines of the program that had been followed in the United Kingdom. It took two and a half months of prodding on our part to elicit from the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Labour and the Prime Minister some indication as to when this program might be presented, and finally after two and a half months what did we get? This anaemic child, this puny child from a government which represents itself as a giant in its vision and in its desire to meet the problem of unemployment.
I say that there is no program this government has brought forward that has brought it into greater disrepute than this particular program, and that it is no credit to a government that should have brought forward serious legislation in the house.

Mr. Chairman, under item one I should like to refer to another matter which is of particular interest to me and which I am sure has far less political significance than what we have just been discussing. It has to do with the dominion bureau of statistics. The dominion bureau of statistics is certainly a very admirable organization. However, I should like to read a resolution which was passed by the county council in my area. It is in these words:
Whereas the number of requests for statistical information with accompanying forms required from municipalities from various government departments is steadily increasing, with accompanying demands on municipal officials.
Whereas these reports increase the work of local staff, necessitating increased personnel with additional cost to the taxpayer. As an example we wish to cite a new monthly form requested under the caption of "Government and Payroll'' requested by the dominion bureau of statistics.
Therefore be it resolved that by unanimous agreement the council of the county of Peterborough in regular session assembled requests the support and co-operation of the dominion and provincial governments in the elimination of duplication and growing volume of statistics required to be filled out by our county and local offices. These reports are increasing the work of local staffs and will certainly require additional staff at our local level in the near future.
This particular resolution was sent to all the counties in Ontario. Within the last couple of weeks or so a stack of letters has been received stating that the councils in all parts of Ontario had unanimously endorsed


this resolution. Certainly, our civilization is becoming more complex. We need more and more research and, therefore, more and more statistics. This is not a political situation at all. This situation would obtain if our friends to the left were in office or if our friends across the aisle were to remain in office.
The point is the municipalities are finding the work extremely burdensome. The problem is not one limited to municipalities and counties but is one which businessmen face as well. I feel it is about time we spent less effort trying to devise new forms and more effort trying to get co-operation between the various government departments. An example of the situation which has developed is seen in one statistical form which requests information be sent to the bureau of statistics which has already been transmitted to the provincial government. This form requires from municipalities certain information concerning debenture debt. The county treasurer has to dig out all the records for the year before to secure the information, and this requires hours and hours of labour. The annoying aspect of the matter is that the information has already been submitted. Indeed, I believe in many cases it has already been published.
One county clerk and treasurer of tremendous ability has estimated that 75 per cent of the information being sent to the dominion bureau of satisfies has already been submitted to the provincial governments or some other organization. We consider of prime importance the matter of the development of secondary industry in this country. I should like to tell this committee something of the work of the industrial development branch which co-ordinates the federal government activities in the industrial development field. It assists Canadian companies considering expansion or seeking new products to manufacture. In addition, the branch seeks out and assists foreign companies interested in establishing plants in Canada.
The branch works closely in carrying out its functions with provincial governments, municipal bodies, business associations and other agencies interested in industrial development. In addition to supplying general information on domestic markets and trade to businessmen, the branch can provide special statistical information on imports and in the past few years has prepared an extensive number of import studies, the most recent being the study of the imports of chemical products. The branch has also been active in promoting licensing arrangements between Canadian and foreign companies. In this connection, it publishes regularly a bulletin entitled "New Methods and Products for Licensing in Canada". Other publications prepared by the branch in response to business requests provide information on taxes, tariffs, sources of financing, forms of business organizations and other matters related to doing business in Canada.
I think the hon. member, and other members, will agree that we are taking this matter very seriously indeed. We are doing everything we can to help new industries become established and to carry on their operations successfully. The branch is ready 90205-6-275i
Supply-Trade and Commerce and willing to receive inquiries, either by mail or in person, from any business firm that wants to come here and talk over matters with us. We believe that the most important means of providing jobs in Canada is by helping the development of secondary industry. I agree with the views expressed by the hon. member last night that this development must be carried forward with all possible speed and I should like to assure him my department will help secondary industry help itself in every possible way we can.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words in connection with this matter, which is one of considerable importance, or at least it has been so described by the government. I should like first of all to refer to a speech made by the Prime Minister on "The Nation's Business" on April 12, 1961. During that speech on television the Prime Minister made the following statement:
For the first time in Canada's history, you, no matter what your racial origin may be, you have the opportunity of registering as a Canadian.
Mr. Chairman, that is not a true statement. That statement is not only inaccurate, but it is false. I think I can demonstrate that from information which I hold in my hand having to do with the decennial census of 1951 when the previous government was in office.
In the questionnaire which I hold in my hand and which was used in the year 1951, heading 16 is entitled "Citizenship (Nationality)", and the first answer given is "Canada". In other words, every Canadian citizen could describe himself in that fashion, as a citizen of Canada, in the census of 1951 and could answer the question truthfully in no other way.
Therefore I say without hesitation that the Prime Minister's statement is simply not in accordance with the facts and he is obviously seeking to claim credit for something with which his government had nothing to do. This, of course, is characteristic of the present government and I feel the record should be corrected in that respect.
I do, however, think that another statement made by the Prime Minister relating to this matter should be put on the record. This


statement can be found at page 749 of Hansard of June 13, 1940. At that time the Prime Minister said:
My criticism of the census is that, regardless of the number of generations that have elapsed or the admixtures of nationality that have taken place during 40, 50, 75 or 125 years, so long as persons must register under the nationality of their paternal ancestor, there will never be that Canadianism which we wish to establish.
I should like to say a word in connection with that statement. In 1940, when the Prime Minister made this statement, he said there would never be a Canadian spirit as long as our citizens were obliged to declare their ethnic origin. I certainly do not agree with that statement. It shows-I say this with all respect-a deep misunderstanding of the history and traditions of the Canadian people.
Of course, we all want to build and develop a united nation, a united and distinctive Canadian nation; but in order to maintain that unity in our country, diversity is also essential and important. Canadians never wanted to follow the policy and attitudes which existed in the United States melting pot, because there cultural diversity has in effect been banished. I believe we want in Canada, as the Leader of the Opposition has said so often, unity without uniformity.
Those two characteristics of the Canadian nation are reflected in questions 8 and 10. Question 8 asks for our nationality and question 10 for our origin. The first one is intended to stress the unity of our people, and I am sure that when question 8 is asked of those who have received their Canadian citizenship they will be very proud indeed to answer that they are Canadians.
Question 10, on the other hand, stresses the element of diversity which can be found in Canada and which most Canadians, I am sure, desire to preserve. This diversity of cultural origin has been in the past, and will be in the future, a great source of cultural enrichment for Canada.
French Canadians are not the only ones who are proud of their cultural ancestry. So are the English, Scots, Irish, Italian, German, Ukrainian and many others. This can be illustrated by the numerous St. Andrew's societies in all parts of Canada.
We want to continue to be informed, as we have in the past, of the composition and cultural origin of all Canadians, because we are convinced that in maintaining cultural diversity we will strengthen the unity of our country. This question, therefore, does not concern only those Canadians of French origin, but all other Canadians. I am convinced that the government was well advised to change its attitude and restore question 10 as it was in 1951, because the object of

this change will prevent any future weakening of that Canadian spirit and unity which all of us in this committee want to see
strengthened.
There is another aspect of this matter. It is that there is provided by this question a great deal of information which otherwise could not be obtained. It seems to me that a census should provide the most complete information about the composition of a people and since there are questions here having to do with age, occupation, marital status, religion, geographical distribution, spoken language and urban and rural density of population, why should there not be a question about racial origin? It is equally important to obtain information as to the racial origin of the individual because this is the only means by which Canadians of all ethnic groups can ascertain their numbers and their distribution across Canada. Why, then, should this question not be asked, since it has been asked since 1891? Why take it away now?
Again, the science of sociology requires that the census reveal the ethnic origin of Canadians. Thanks to the information which has been obtained from this question in the census it has been possible for sociologists to prepare and write works of great importance upon the concentration and the diversity of population in urban as well as rural areas. What Mr. St. Laurent said in 1951, which was characteristic of his approach to problems of this kind, was that this is a free country and if anyone wants to declare his origin as Canadian, no one would stop him because we do not have a dictatorship. However, I have great objection, Mr. Chairman, to this being done by those people who are in a position to use this material for political purposes.
I believe the Canadian people, and certainly the newspapers of this country, should be violently upset about this. The newspapers should request some type of protection for the Canadian people. Some of this information
Supply-Trade and Commerce
does not even appear in income tax forms. If it is going to be asked for, then the government will have to respect the secrecy. There should be an assurance given to the people that the government is not going to secure this information through the people it has appointed. I have suggested that the four commissioners appointed in my area are all political people, people who are not only conscious of politics-as we wish everybody to be -but are actively engaged in working with one political party. They have been appointed and are being paid as political patronage. This is wrong. I do not believe this situation is conducive to the judicious handling of the census and will not result in the full and reasonable disclosure of the business of each and every one of the Canadian people.
