I think we have just heard one of the most irresponsible statements heard in this chamber for a long time. This is the kind of speech you expect to hear in a place other than the parliament of Canada. I am rather shocked that the hon. member should have delivered such a speech. According to the hon. gentleman, you cannot trust anybody in his riding but him.
The people who have been chosen to carry out this most important task of taking the census are very highly respected people in all parts of the country, otherwise they would not have been chosen. They have been chosen on the basis, first of all of a good education; professional or business experience in a supervisory capacity; knowledge of the district; tact; good judgment and ability to deal with the people.
The hon. member has spoken about the matter of secrecy. If we can believe what he says, the information that these census takers have been gathering will be used only for their own information, for their own, personal gain. This is one of the most ridiculous statements I have ever heard, and I have heard quite a few. This matter of secrecy is dealt with in the Statistics Act. I should like to quote from section 15 of that act, as follows:

Supply-Trade and Commerce
No individual return and no part of an individual return made, and no answer to any question put, for the purposes of this act, shall,... be published ...
It has been mentioned, too, that the census taker takes an oath of secrecy. An oath of secrecy is a very serious matter. It is not something people take lightly. The people who have been chosen are serious and respectable people, and when they take an oath of secrecy they are doing so in a very serious way.
I should like to mention the penalties that are imposed on any of those who are census takers and who break these regulations so far as secrecy is concerned. The penalties are outlined in section 34 of the Statistics Act as follows:
Every person employed in the execution of any duty under this act or any regulation who,
(a)	after having taken the prescribed oath, deserts from his duty, or wilfully makes any false declaration, statement or return touching any such matter;
(b)	in the pretended performance of his duties thereunder, obtains or seeks to obtain information that he is not duly authorized to obtain; or
(c)	fails to keep inviolate the secrecy of the information gathered or entered on the schedules and forms, and who, except as allowed by this act and the regulations, divulges the contents of any schedule or form filled in, in pursuance of this act or any regulation, or any information furnished in pursuance of this act or any regulation; is guilty of an offence and is liable, on summary conviction, to a fine not exceeding three hundred dollars, or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months, or to both fine and imprisonment.
I think I have outlined very clearly the qualifications of these people. I think I have made it clear that they have been chosen with great care. They are very highly respected people in their communities. They are given a very strict code of ethics to guide them in the performance of their duty. If any of them should not perform that duty properly, there are penalties prescribed. As I say, they are all required to take an oath of secrecy. People of the calibre of those who have been chosen to carry out this important task take an oath of secrecy as a serious matter.
I do not believe I have to deal with this matter any further, Mr. Chairman. I think the remarks of the hon. member were in extremely poor taste. I think the hon. member is casting a reflection, in a completely unjustified way, on the very fine people across this country who are going to be carrying out a very important task indeed. I can assure the hon. member and the people of Canada that in my view this census will be taken well and none of the things which dwell in his imagination will take place.
If there is any instance of anything of this kind taking place, there are very definite

rules, regulations and penalties prescribed for them. I very much hope that none of these penalties will be needed. I do not think they will.
I hope we will not again hear this kind of speech from the hon. member or any other hon. member. The hon. member's remarks were derogatory and unfair to those people who are chosen to carry out such an important task in the future.

speechtext:
On item 401, I have recommended action on other occasions to permit the amendment of the National Energy Board Act by incorporating in it section 273 of the Railway Act. When the National Energy Board Act was passed in 1959, section 273 of the Railway Act was omitted. The National Energy Board Act includes sections 207 to 246 and section 248 of the Railway Act but section 273 was omitted. The sections of the Railway Act which were included in the National Energy Board Act deal with the acquisition and expropriation of land for purposes of right of way.
The amendment would make pipe lines at present under federal charter subject to provincial drainage laws in the same way as pipe lines which operate under provincial charter. Pipe lines involved in municipal drainage schemes would be treated like those of any other property owner, being subject to assessment and so on. Their owners would enjoy the right of appeal to the courts if they wish to have such assessments adjusted. Owners of pipe lines would be made responsible for any added cost to a municipal drainage scheme caused by their presence or operations.
The provisions which are requested to be incorporated in the Railway Act would be of great assistance to individual farmers and municipal drainage schemes especially in the area of southwestern Ontario which I represent. This proposal to include section 273 of the Railway Act in the National Energy Board Act came to me from the drainage engineering firm of Archibald, Gray and McKay of London on behalf of the township of Adelaide. This request has been endorsed by the association of Ontario land surveyors,

by the Middlesex county council, by the Ontario minister of highways acting in his capacity as chairman of the special committee of the Ontario legislature which was set up to inquire into expropriation proceedings for land in Ontario, by the township of East Williams, by the Ontario federation of agriculture and by the township of London, Middlesex county.
I intend to let one or two of these endorsers argue the case for me. The association of Ontario land suveyors at its meeting held in Hamilton on February 15, 16 and 17, 1960 passed a resolution endorsing this proposal. May I say that this association is an important body whose members undertake the engineering in connection with most of the drainage work carried on in the province of Ontario. I intend to read an excerpt from the report of this annual meeting. It refers to a question which is the second of a series of questions placed before the meeting for endorsation by the drainage committee of the association. The excerpt reads as follows:

The second question is rather
involved, and I shall try to explain the question before I read it. Under subsection 22 of section 8 of the Municipal Drainage Act, public utilities are responsible for the increased cost of drainage work caused by the construction and operation of such public utilities. There is some doubt as to the application of this subsection where a public utility holds a dominion charter. Railways were made responsible for the increased cost of a drain caused by the operation of the railway company by an amendment to the Railway Act early in the twentieth century-see section 273 of the Railway Act. Recently we have had a number of oil pipe lines and gas pipe lines constructed across our province, and a number of these pipe line companies operate under a dominion charter. So we are up against the problem: are these companies responsible for the additional costs of drainage work caused by their operations? Certain sections of the Railway Act were incorporated in the Pipe Lines Act, but this all important section 273, which made the railway companies liable for the increased cost in drainage work, was omitted. Last fall the National Energy Board Act was passed, and section 71, subsection 1 of that act. incorporates sections 207-246, and also section 248, of the Railway Act but this all important section 273 was left out.
The question now is: "Should section 71, subsection 1, of the National Energy Board Act be amended by the addition of section 273 of the Railway Act to read-'Sections 207-246, 248 and 273 of the Railway Act'; in other words should these pipe line companies be responsible for the increased costs to drainage work caused by their operation?" The committee's answer to this question is: "Yes". And we would recommend that this association go on record as being in favour of this amendment to the existing legislation. I move the adoption of the committee's answer to this report with this request.
Later that report was adopted at the annual meeting of the Ontario association of land surveyors.

At the last session of the legislature of Ontario a select committee was appointed to investigate and inquire into the laws of expropriation in this province. I have had the privilege of being appointed chairman of the select committee and it is in that capacity that I wish to bring to your attention a problem which was placed before the select committee.
I am advised that a submission has been made to you by W. H. A. Thomas, Esq. the member of parliament for Middlesex West, requesting that the National Energy Board Act be amended so as to make section 273 of the Railway Act of Canada applicable to pipe line companies incorporated under the provisions of federal legislation. As you are probably already aware, the above mentioned section of the Railway Act would make the pipe line companies responsible for any interference with drainage in the provinces as are any railways, public utilities or other such bodies; the problem would appear to be so reasonable that one would almost think that the omission was accidental rather than intentional. The interference which may be created in both municipal and provincial drainage schemes by the construction of a pipe line is very serious and can in certain circumstances cause great expense to both local land owners and the ratepayers of the province.
On behalf of the select committee may I urgently request that this proposed amendment receive your favourable consideration and, ultimately, submission to parliament for its consideration.
We have the anomalous situation in Middlesex West of four pipe lines crossing the riding, three operating under Ontario provincial charter and one under national charter. In respect of the three, when a farm or municipal drain has to be carried across the pipe line the pipe line company is compelled to pay the cost of such crossing. However, in respect of the fourth, which operates under federal charter, the pipe line company does not have to pay for the crossing. The practice of the national energy board has been to award these crossing permits with the expense to be borne by the municipal drainage authority. I should mention that costs of drainage crossings have run as high as $7,000 to $8,000 each. I would suggest that it is unreasonable to have pipe lines in one area operating under similar conditions treated in different ways.
Without taking any more time I would urge upon the minister the necessity for expedition in the consideration which is now being given this matter by the national energy board, and would suggest that an amendment be made to the National Energy Board Act incorporating section 273 of the Railway Act.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take a moment of the committee's time to say a word about the energy board itself. I should like to congratulate the members of that board and the chairman, as well as its staff, for the manner in which they have carried out their function since the board's establishment. Their success is certainly a great credit to themselves and to the system which was introduced in the establishing of the National Energy Board Act. I know that all hon. members of the committee, as well as members of the petroleum industry and consumer alike, agree that this has been a very successful operation.
I am sure the minister is aware that in a very short time the term of office of the

present chairman of the board will expire. I believe that office of the present incumbent carries a two year term. I do not suggest that the other members of the board are not capable of replacing the present chairman but, in the interest of the board and in view of the chairman's past experience, I suggest it would be desirable that the government negotiate with the province of Alberta so that Mr. McKinnon's appointment can be extended for another two year period. I realize that there are difficulties in this connection but I am sure the members of the board would be the first to concur that this would be a good step.
I would like to say a word about the national oil and gas policy which is adminis-

tered by the board. I had the privilege in 1957 of expressing in this house the hope that I would some day see the establishment of a national oil and gas policy, and the development of a program which would encourage the industry to voluntarily correct its own problems by increasing the domestic and foreign markets for Canadian crude oil. This government's administration in this regard adopted the lesser of two severe policies, on the one hand to take no action at all and allow the industry to find its own level, or to establish fairly severe control for imports of oil. While I have always advocated the eventual construction of a pipe line, I nevertheless agree that the course followed by the board in introducing a voluntary program is more appropriately suited to the present need. As has been pointed out, this program will provide a level of production, in terms of barrels that the construction of a pipe line would produce in the two year period yet to elapse.
What I do ask the minister and the chairman of the energy board, however, is that when they are making assessments in the future for targets beyond 1963, they make the calculations well in advance based on the returns of oil company refineries. We should keep in mind the factor of growth which is going to be substantial; for I am inclined to believe that while the present policy has been a sound one the targets were perhaps a bit low. Nevertheless there is no question that the policy as such has provided tremendous benefits to the industry, first of all by providing orderly regulation of oil production in the producing areas by establishing, of course, firm contracts for the marketing of oil not only in Canada but in terms of United States markets as well.
It has been said in this house and outside that to some degree this policy is going to be dependent on our success in moving oil into the United States. I hope that this is not entirely true, but quite obviously if the policy is to be successful it will have to work on the assumption that we are going to be able to sell more oil in the Ontario market and thus replace crude oil from foreign sources. I am happy to be able to say that indications are that the Ontario market has shown the largest increase we have seen for some time, an increase of 20,000 barrels a day over the same period one year ago.
What is also particularly significant is that many people who said that this policy could not work now agree that it is not only going to work but it has already proved successful in terms of total production. The first six months indicate there is no doubt that the target will be reached. In fact we are not too far off the total target for the year.
Supply-Trade and Commerce Therefore, I say to the minister that he and his colleagues should be congratulated on introducing a policy which in the long run is going to assist the industry. I say to him that in making assessments for the future, in so far as targets are concerned, we must be absolutely certain that we relate the total targets to the development of the industry and that we do not in any way underestimate this development and thus make the targets for the future too low.
The other point I should like to make is that there are a number of areas which concern the government's relation to the petroleum and natural gas industry. In the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys we have a very effective geological survey. The Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources administers legislation and regulations relating to Canadian oil and gas. I will argue, as I have done before, that in this parliament we should attempt to put all of these matters having to do with hydrocarbons, in fact all of the energy sources, under one department and one administration to avoid duplication of effort and to be able to build up a staff which can adequately look after the problems related to the industry, because I know some of the difficulties in obtaining staff for the national energy board and, of course, for the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. I would hope that some day we shall see the national energy board having authority over the Canada oil and gas regulations; for it would only seem logical that this phase of the oil development program should come under one particular division.
I wish to make it very clear that I am not suggesting any minister of the crown have the responsibility for all of this; I am merely saying that we should give some thought to taking all the segments of the petroleum and gas industry and putting them under a single responsibility, as has been done in a great many countries similar to Canada.
Finally, may I say to the minister and to the board that I am certain when the minister expresses his belief that this policy could work he should nevertheless emphasize that if the targets are not reached the government will have no other course but to, as I understand it, implement section 87 of the energy board authority. This is indeed assurance enough to the petroleum industry and the people of Canada as a whole that the government intends to make its policy work and in this we congratulate the minister and wish him every success.

Mr. Chairman, on April 21, I think it was, I was just on the point of quoting an excerpt from the fifth volume pubished by the Societe historique de Saint-Boniface when the chairman called it five o'clock.
I am speaking in French tonight because the other day, the brief remarks I made in English were ascribed to the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) and since the hon. member speaks only one language, I do not think there will be any mistake this time.
The excerpt I wanted to quote the other day-it is on page 29 of volume 5 which I have just mentioned-was from a letter written by Msgr. Tache, then bishop of St. Boniface. In that letter, Bishop Tache refers to the building which had been constructed before 1846 for the reception of the Grey Nuns. Here is what Bishop Tache had to say:
The deeply Christian families of St. Boniface find satisfaction in the fact that their daughters enjoy educational facilities similar to those available to their sons.
IMr. Broome.]
The Sisters of Charity, or Grey Nuns, operate a school for girls in St. Boniface: by a special Providence, those devoted nuns were able to erect a large and beautiful building entirely for educational purposes.
They have a boarding school and a day school, and they train teachers in their normal school; 18 nuns are full-time teachers and 300 children attend the classes.
Our laws on education, so sound and in keeping with the real sense of freedom, promote the Christian education of our young people.
This is what Bishop Tache could say in 1888 about our education laws. Unfortunately, the situation has changed a great deal since 1890, but I believe that one day the education system in Manitoba will be restored to what it was in 1888.
Referring in his letter to charitable works, Bishop Tache mentioned this:
Charitable activities cannot be wanting wherever there are Sisters of Charity.
The old building, birthplace of those organizations in St. Boniface, is still the same one which was erected by Msgr. Provencher. It is Vicarial House in which the novitiate is located and around which eventually were built an orphanage, a home for disabled women and a hospital.
Now, this house, already described as an old one in 1888 by Bishop Tache, is I believe the oldest house in western Canada. It is located on Tache street in St. Boniface.
I am happy to learn that the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources is giving earnest attention to this historic building. I understand certain amounts will be voted for its preservation.
The house has been entrusted to a museum committee in St. Boniface. I am not sure, but I also think that the city of St. Boniface is prepared to vote a substantial amount for the conversion of this house into a museum, and for its maintenance.
I hope the government of the province of Manitoba will do likewise so as to help preserve this historic building.
I believe that monuments and museums are important to keep alive the history of a nation.
In my view, the history of the province of Manitoba ranks with that of any other area in America. We remember that La Verendrye in 1735, had already travelled over most of the territory of the prairies. We know that settlers who came over from Scotland in 1812, 1813 and 1815 developed that area.
Manitoba has many historians, for example, Father Dugas, one Mr. Tasse, Alexander Ross, Joseph James Hargrave, Donald Gunn, Alexander Begg, George Bryce, R. B. Hill, F. H. Schofield, Miss Margaret McWilliams and Mr. W. L. Morton, a professor at the university.

Apart from the historical society of St. Boniface, I think there is in Winnipeg an historical society which also has been interested in the history of the province of Manitoba.
Mr. Chairman, I think it is most important for the citizens of the province of Manitoba, as well as for all Canadians, to have some knowledge of the history of the province of Manitoba. In fact, if the history of that province were better known to Canadians, it would be easier to maintain harmony in this country.
When those hardy Scotch pioneers came to Canada, they stopped at York Factory, in the fall of 1811. They were able to spend the winter there before proceeding on their trip to the Red river which they reached only the following autumn.
Since winter was too cold and food was lacking, they had to establish quarters 70 miles south of Red river, in the village of Pembina, where the population was almost exclusively French Metis. In order to survive, those Scotch settlers had, on three occasions, to seek shelter with those French Metis of Pembina. However, one year there was a shortage of food even in that village and all the settlers, men, women and children alike, had to make for the prairies, in the snow, so as to try to find a group of Metis hunters who might provide them with shelter and food.
That is what those pioneers did.
I might add that one year there was so much snow that horses could not be used on the prairies, the buffaloes had wandered away and the people of Pembina village could not survive. They, in turn, had to seek food from the Scotch pioneers who, having become farmers, had managed to keep enough wheat and flour to save the other settlement from starvation.
This lesson from history proves that people need one another and that if the descendants of those Scotch pioneers are still living today, it is thanks to the help their forefathers received from the people of those villages who numbered about 500 in 1821. It is true that the Scottish pioneers were somewhat less numerous but, by helping one another they managed to beat the great poverty and depression that prevailed in those days.
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to dwell overlong on that subject. I simply wish to thank the minister for what he has already done and urge him to solve the problem, to try to obtain for the citizens of St. Boni-
Supply-Northern Affairs face that house where we may preserve, before they are all lost, the historical records we now have in our possession.
Mr. Chairman, while there have been many historians of that period it may be pointed out also that there was a poet by the name of Pierre Falcon, who once lived in Pembina and who later moved to a place called While Horse Plains, which in 1824 became St. Frangois-Xavier.
That poet wrote songs on all the great historic events that took place in the province at that time. I therefore feel that someday we might consider erecting a monument to that first poet of western Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to join the hon. member for St. Boniface in his appeal to the minister for the aid of the historic sites and monuments board and the other facilities of his department in the preservation of the relics of the early history of the Canadian west before it was even Canadian. I do so with a certain amount of local pride. As an old schoolboy of Tache high school in St. Boniface, I know these places very well. I know, I think, every alley and every street in that oldest city west of the lakes. There is so much there that is worth preserving and that is a monument of the fact that, after some initial difficulty, we have developed in that community a bonne entente which has not only been very satisfactory in that community but which has resulted in the production from that community of some of the most talented people in the French language in all Canada today.
Indeed, I would go so far as to say, if it would not be regarded as too boastful coming from one who spent 30 years of his life in Manitoba, that perhaps the French speaking inhabitants of Manitoba, in proportion to their numbers in this generation, have produced a disproportionately large number of remarkable and distinguished people in the arts and letters of this country. Of course, one thinks particularly of Gabrielle Roy, of Gisele MacKenzie, in another field, and of her brother who is now distinguishing himself as well. One could go on, of course, and add to this list.

I should like to go on and remind hon. members that the very beginning of our whole country was in the constituency that I represent. It does seem to me that the time has come to commemorate, in a proper way, the landfall of the discoverer of Canada, John Cabot, at Cape Bonavista, on St. John's day in 1497.
I suggest to the minister it would also be most appropriate to commemorate the fact that that later explorer of Canada, that mariner from St. Malo, Jacques Cartier, following a generation later in the wake of John Cabot, made his first landfall at Cape Bonavista. Before he went to Gaspe and long before he went to Quebec, Cartier trod the soil of Newfoundland.
This fact should be commemorated as part of our history, as is the case in any part of this country where the historic sites and monuments board or the historic section of the national parks board, commemorate these things. It not only has a cultural value, but it also has a very practical, hard material value. The commemoration of these ancient monuments is one of the greatest of the many current attractions in this country. The more we mark these sites, the more we advertise them, the more we can hope to make our country interesting and attractive, not merely to our own people who travel about but also to those who come to visit us from other countries.
I might point out to the minister that since a national park was established in Newfoundland by the previous administration, the present government has made great improvements there for which I am grateful. I would emphasize to the minister the fact that, in a sense, this gratitude is a lively anticipation of future improvements because only the surface has been scratched. This national park has resulted in the completion of the road right across the whole of Newfoundland. Gander, on one side of that park, is the crossroads of the whole world and Bonavista, on the other side of the park, is the site of the beginning of the history of North America. What would be more fitting than that tours should be arranged for those people who are held up in Gander. It is only 100 miles across the park to Bonavista where one finds the most beautiful scenery, I was going to say in all North America, but at any rate east of the rockies.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I listened with close attention this afternoon to the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Regnier) and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill).
The latter referred to Jacques Cartier and suggested that he first landed in Newfoundland. At first I had some doubts, but having later done some research in my office, I have found that he actually did set foot in Newfoundland, although the exact spot is not mentioned.
The French explorer Jacques Cartier made his first trip to Canada in April 1534. We find in his memoirs the first fragments of Cana-

dian history. After a brief stop for fresh water somewhere along the north shore of the St. Lawrence-and I am prepared to believe the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate, because I seem to have read somewhere that it might have been in Newfoundland-he sailed in a southwesterly direction, along the Magdalen islands and Prince Edward Island, and finally stopped on the shores of the Baie de Chaleur, though historians have never determined the exact location. The presence of seemingly hostile Indians prevented him from landing, however, and Cartier's narrative indicates that his ships turned back toward the north on July 12. On July 24, they entered another deep bay, and Cartier thought it was the basin through which the St. Lawrence flowed into the sea; he thought it was the road to Cathay. Having gone ashore to explore the area, he realized his mistake. He now felt certain he had just discovered a new continent. So he had his men build a wooden cross 30 feet high, bearing a shield with an engraved fleur-de-lis and the words "Vive le roi de France" written in large gothic script. Here is how Cartier himself describes the scene in the French language of the time:
On the XXIII day of said month, we built a cross 30 feet in height, which was constructed in the presence of a large number of them on the cape at the entrance to the said cove. Under the cross-arm of that cross we put a shield in relief bearing three fleurs-de-lis, and on the cross we put a wooden sign bearing the words LONG LIVE THE KING OF FRANCE. And the said cross we set up on the said cape before them while they watched us make it and set it up. After it was raised, we all fell to our knees with clasped hands adoring it in their presence, and making signs at them, looking at the cross and pointing to the sky, to signify to them that said cross was the sign of our redemption, at what they expressed much admiration, turning to look at the said cross.
It is regrettable that that cross was not made of material more durable than wood, because, soon after, it was destroyed by the elements. The actual location where that cross was erected is not known even today. It is however admitted by all historians that it was on the shores of what we now call the bay of Gaspe. The place which seems to best meet the descriptions of this event and on which many of our earlier historians agree, is now called Peninsula point, a small headland with sandy beaches which juts out at the mouth of the bay of Gaspe. Any navigator would probably choose this place to rest before venturing further into these unknown and unexplored lands.
The erection of this cross is a memorable event. To all those who want to keep an historical souvenir of this country's origins and
Supply[DOT]-Northern Affairs who hope to see the writing of a history enriched with glorious events, Cartier's gesture marks a starting point. The great cross set up by the French navigator when he discovered our country was soon buried in the sand, but the memory of the moving ceremony that took place in the imposing scenery of the verdant forest under a blue sky will always remain vivid in the minds of Canadians. It was one of the most sublime moments of all our history. And in a developing country such as ours, it is an inheritance that all generations must cherish jealously.
We should not be ashamed to show devotion for our origins, because a nation is not founded only on material things. And to forget those gestures of the past, or still to deprive Canadians of this worthy heritage of history, is to hold our birthright in contempt.
In the years between 1534 and 1625, when France was trying to colonize this new land, the bay of Gaspe was often mentioned in the memoirs and writings of the time as a mooring place for ships from foreign countries.
After their hazardous crossing of the Atlantic in their frail crafts, the captains of yore headed for the bay of Gaspe, where the crew traded various items with the Indians for food and water.
Once the crew was rested, the ship weighed anchor and, from Gaspe headed for Quebec or Montreal.

These are facts I picked up in various books and also obtained from historians who were doing research work in Gaspe, and they let me have reports on well established facts. That is why I dare quote them, because I want to inform the house as accurately as possible of some details which sometimes are rather complex and difficult to establish. Of course, I want to avoid errors. I am therefore quoting, if I may, details gathered here and there.
Thus, in the very beginning of our history, Gaspe constantly played an important part in the first attempts at colonization of this new continent.
Indeed, it has been mentioned that the greatest naval battle of our history was fought in the bay of Gaspe. That same battle had forced Champlain to surrender Quebec

Supply-Northern Affairs to the British, in 1629, and certainly did contribute to change the course of Canadian history.
Mr. Chairman, there are several other historic events connected with the Gaspe peninsula.
Alas, that part of our homeland, which is legendary and basic to our history, has been too much neglected until today.
I very well remember that at the little rural school I attended as a boy, we used to study Canadian history in a textbook in which could be found the following words written under a photo:
Gaspe, Jacques Cartier. Cartier plants a cross. There was also this inscription:
Long live the King of France.
What I find strange today is the fact that we are questioning the actual place where Cartier landed.
Mr. Chairman, all those who have studied their history and who want to recognize that part of their province for what it is really worth, admit that it was actually in Gaspe that Jacques Cartier landed.
There are also several other historic facts I should like to point out. Among those, there is the one where it is said that later, in the course of our history, the British army, under General Wolfe, encamped at Gaspe before capturing Quebec for the second time in 1759. On September 4, 1758, Wolfe arrived there with seven ships and three infantry regiments numbering 1,500 men. Those soldiers settled on the wide and triangular belts of sand of Peninsula point: the historic site where, in all likelihood, Cartier landed in 1534.
The proof of this occupancy is provided by a painting of Captain Hervey Smith who served as aide-de-camp to General Wolfe on that trip. The painting shows the exact location of buildings in that group, including the two-storey building known as the Customs house, where Wolfe lived during his stay in Gaspe. An important historical fact is that the location of General Wolfe's house was determined accurately by the late Fred Richmond, of Gaspe, who discovered the remains of a fireplace at the exact spot indicated on Captain Smith's painting.
Several of the relics buried at that place indicate that the station was inhabited in the past by French traders. A coin found on the site of the "Maison des Douanes" was a gold piece clearly bearing the date 1693.


Three two-sou pieces from 1629, or even from 1575, were also found on this spot.
Mr. Chairman, I could relate many other legendary facts, but I would not want to take too much of the time of the house. I might have another opportunity to speak on it at length.
But, as a son of Gaspe, and as the representative of Gaspe, I am proud of this part of our province.
And I also take pride in proclaiming in this house that Gaspe has made a major contribution to our history.
When, every summer, I see many tourists come to visit the Gaspe peninsula, to see for themselves what they have learned in their history books, who are filled with admiration by the scenic beauty of a site such as Perce, I wonder if each and everyone of us, rising above political considerations, should not acknowledge at least inwardly, if we do not want to express this feeling outwardly, that we have too long neglected and ignored that part of our province which is called Gaspe.
To think that after all these years, we do not even have a historic park in Gaspe that displays all these marvels.
Every summer, I meet people in my riding, members of the Catholic clergy, the bishop of Gaspe, Protestant ministers, and I am glad to note that there exists full cooperation between these various groups.
In my part of the country there is no class, racial or religious discrimination.
The town of Gaspe has a population equally comprised of French and English Canadians. The parish of Douglastown is entirely Irish. Not a word of French is heard there. The parish of Barachois is also English speaking.
And yet, each and everyone of us is working in harmony, because we are all proud of our history, and our hearts are filled with love for the Gaspe peninsula, our province and our beloved country, Canada.
Mr. Chairman, that is why-no matter what may be thought by those who feel I am delaying the adoption of the estimates-I considered it my duty to express the voice of Gaspe for in 1957, the people of that area put their confidence in me, regardless of political considerations, because they examined my record and knew my attachment for the Gaspe land. The confidence they put in me indicates that they wanted me to come here to Ottawa, not only to listen to debates, but.

Mr. Chairman, I hope that what I am saying now will not be in vain but that it will bring results. My duty as a member is not to come to this House of Commons and accept everything without saying a word; I feel I am entitled to obtain for that part of the Gaspe peninsula what it has a right to expect.
The population of the Gaspe peninsula has always contributed to the progress of Canada. If some one answers that it is not certain that Cartier ever landed at Gaspe, I do not accept that. It is my privilege not to do so.
If you only knew how many hours and how many years I have spent studying Gas-pesia and its history. I have been a professor in Quebec for ten years and I like to think that the history I taught my pupils was not false history, as some people claim. Anyhow unless I am given proof to the contrary, I am going to continue to teach that splendid history.
Mr. Chairman, I want to apologize, perhaps I have been a bit too long. No matter how long my political career might last, how many years or days I might spend here in Ottawa, I would like people to say after I am gone, after I have left Ottawa, that at least I have made known my Gaspesia, that I have claimed what it has a right to expect from our government and that I have accomplished my duty. That is the only reward I am expecting from politics.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
-I can commence my remarks by saying that the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources under its young and energetic minister is beginning to play a more important role throughout all parts of Canada than it ever has before. This development is taking place throughout every province of Canada, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and has made its impression upon my own riding of Queens-Lunenburg in Nova Scotia.
I should first like to join with my colleagues, as well as with members of the opposition, in extending congratulations to the minister upon his appointment to this portfolio. The former minister plotted a firm course to be followed, but I am pleased to note that the present minister has taken a keen interest in all matters pertaining to his department and its administration, and is making further improvements upon the good plans established by his predecessor.
Previous speakers have pointed out the fact that Canada is showing a substantial deficit in her tourist trade with the United States, and it is to the Canadian government travel bureau branch of the department and the national parks branch that I shall direct

most of my remarks. As a Nova Scotian I am fully aware of the impact made upon our economy by the tourist industry, and of the necessity of attracting to Canada and to our particular area a larger number of tourists.
A study of the tourist survey of Nova Scotia as carried out by the Nova Scotia travel bureau in 1960, indicates that the tourist industry is big business, especially in our province. It gives some idea of the factors which influenced tourists to visit Nova Scotia. According to the survey, tourist booklets influence over 52 per cent while magazine and newspaper advertising were effective in encouraging another 35 per cent to visit Nova Scotia. These figures would indicate that tourists will come to your area if you intelligently and carefully promote the beauty spots and historic sites which are to be seen during a visit, and the quality of the hotel and motel accommodations and the variety of sites to be seen will determine the length of their stay.
On February 8, 1961, the hon. E. A. Manson, minister of trade and industry in Nova Scotia stated:
In I960 Nova Scotia's tourist industry achieved new records, both in the number of visitors to the province and in the amount of money they spent.
After studies extending back over four years and intensified in 1960, a revised and corrected system of gathering tourist statistics shows that the number of visitors to Nova Scotia during the four summer months of 1960 totalled 586,111, and their estimated expenditures were $48,328,733.
He further stated:
Canadian and American averages obtained from the 1960 registration card inquiries for the "Order of the Good Time", weighted on the basis of 73 per cent Canadian and 27 per cent American traffic, has led to the conclusion that the value of spending by tourists from other Canadian provinces this year was $30,773,902 and by American visitors, $17,554,830.
Mr. Manson said that Nova Scotia was fortunate in having tourist statistics reaching back, with an interruption during the war years, to 1922. There could be no doubt that the long term trend in Nova Scotia's tourist traffic was sharply upward.
This, of course, is most encouraging.
I was especially pleased to note the minister's comments on the resources for tomorrow conference scheduled to take place in Montreal next October and the fact that water pollution will be a subject for discussion. When we consider the effect of polluted water upon the health of our people and its destructive power in the salmon and inland fisheries as well as the partial destruction of the shellfish industry along our coast especially near the mouths of our rivers, only then do we realize the importance of the legislation introduced by the government to provide assistance to municipalities for the construction of sewage disposal facilities. This is a great forward step, one that was long overdue, and 90205-6-276
Supply-Northern Affairs in view of the importance of our inland fisheries as a tourist attraction I hope it will be possible for federal and provincial fishery conservation officers, as well as municipal wardens and industrial leaders, to attend this conference and outline any further ideas they may have on this important problem.
In the last decade Canadians have spent twice as much money travelling in the United States and abroad compared with the money spent in Canada by Americans and tourists from foreign lands. Our Canadian tourist deficit is an important part of our over-all balance of payments deficit. For a long time the Canadian Manufacturers' Association has been promoting the slogan, "buy Canadian". I think the time has come to adopt another slogan, "Sell Canadian"-"Sell Canada". In view of the benefits that accrue from the tourist industry, not only to private industry but to the federal and provincial governments as well, I believe that government has a responsibility to promote tourism on a national level. These efforts would pay a sizeable dividend in that the expenditures of tourists from other countries would materially benefit our balance of payments position.
Why do Canadians want to visit the United States, the United Kingdom or, for that matter, Paris? I submit that one reason is to visit the historic sites they have previously only seen in pictures or heard about in song or story. Here is a challenge to the new Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources to renew in greater number the historic sites and national parks throughout Canada and especially those in Nova Scotia for the benefit of foreign as well as Canadian tourists. At the present time a start has been made in Nova Scotia with the national park in Cape Breton. It is undoubtedly one of the beauty spots of Canada providing every facility for the visiting tourist. However, I believe there is room in Nova Scotia for another national park and for further development of historic sites, and I believe that some of this should be along the south shore of Nova Scotia.
It is my understanding that the minister plans to visit Nova Scotia this summer and I would welcome the opportunity to show him some of the areas worth developing in my riding. Time will not permit me to mention all the historic sites but we could start at Port Mouton in Queen's county. Here we would see where the French explorer De-Monts first landed at this port in 1604 and established a settlement prior to sailing up the bay of Fundy to Annapolis. We are told that the port received its name because a sheep jumped overboard and was nearly drowned before it was rescued.

Supply-Northern Affairs
In the same year DeMonts entered another harbour which he named Port Rossignol and which retained that name until the new England settlers came in 1759 and 1760 and renamed it Liverpool after the same port in England. During the war of 1812 between the United States and Great Britain, Liverpool became famous as the home of the privateers operating under letters of marque that were granted by the government. One of the earlier privateer owners was a member of the Nova Scotia house of assembly. His name was Mr. Simeon Perkins. On our tour we could visit his home recently restored through the efforts of the historical society of Liverpool and the provincial government.
Another site worth visiting would be fort Point at Liverpool which was originally called fort Morris. It was here in 1773 that Simeon Perkins really distinguished himself. The fort was captured by an American privateer when the British garrison was asleep. Simeon Perkins organized the militia, captured the captain of the American privateer and worked out an agreement whereby he regained control of the fort in exchange for the captain.
Leaving Liverpool we travel along the south shore to Petite Riviere and cape La-have near the mouth of the Lahave river. DeMonts and Champlain in 1604 named it Cap de la Have. In 1632 Isaac DeRazilly fortified it and brought in settlers and in 1670 it was captured by the English and resurrendered to the French. In 1720 Sir William Phips thought of Lahave as a government seat, so we readily see the importance attached to this area in that day.
Travelling through Bridgewater, a town of rare beauty on the Lahave river, with outstanding shopping and tourist accommodations, we next visit Lunenburg, the home of the Bluenose. This famous ship made international racing history and many American tourists come to this town to see the shipbuilding yards where this ship was built. Not only was the Bluenose constructed there but also there was recently constructed for Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer a replica of the Bounty which was made famous in the book, "Mutiny on the Bounty". Here too we can see the site of the old blockhouse built in 1773 by the Hanoverian settlers as a protection from the Indians on what is now called blockhouse hill. At the present the local Lions club is actively interested in restoring this blockhouse and I would urge the minister to give earnest consideration to the restoration of this national historic site as well as those I have previously mentioned.
I am certain the minister will find very few places in Canada as storied and as interesting as Lunenburg county. Near Lunen-

burg town is a place called the Ovens that has long been an attraction to tourists. They are deep caverns worn in the sides of the rocky cliffs, the largest of which is about 18 feet in height and 40 or more feet in depth. The sea is never still and rushes into these caverns making a noise like the report of a heavy cannon. Huge gold discoveries were made here in 1861 and many claims were staked.
In Lunenburg county you will also find the towns of Mahone Bay and Chester and along the coast separating these two towns there are over 300 islands. One of these is widely known as Oak island, famous for the treasures supposed to have been buried there by the famous pirate, Captain Kidd. It was also in Mahone Bay in the year 1813 that the American privateer, Young Teazer, pursued by a man of war, was blown up by a deserter from the British service. It is rumoured to this day that on a foggy night this ship, with its sails flapping in the breeze, can still be seen on the horizon. It is called "the ghost of the flying Dutchman".
At Chester, Nova Scotia, American tourists have already established a large tourist colony due to the fact that the scenery in this area could safely be classed among the most beautiful in the world. Farther along the coast we come to Blandford, first settled by the Irish around 1809. This peninsula is famous for its sandy beaches and its high rise of land called "aspotogan", an old Micmac Indian name, which is approximately 500 feet above sea level and is a landmark for navigators. This area would be exceptionally well suited for a second national park and I hope the minister and his officials will take a careful look at the Blandford district as well as others I have mentioned during our tour of this area. I might add that the minister's visit will be very much improved over any that might have been made in the years when this country was under Liberal rule for I know of no road in Canada that was in worse state than was the Blandford road during those years. However, as a result of the roads to resources program, I am pleased to state that the Blandford road has been under construction, and in a few years it will stand as a monument to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources and his program.
From these remarks hon. members can readily see the many attractions and points of interest my riding in Nova Scotia offers the tourist. At the moment we have a Canadian government travel bureau or tourist office in New York City, one in Chicago and one opening in San Francisco. My riding alone offers points of interest to English, French, German, Swiss, Scots and Irish, to

mention a few, and in this day of jet travel I believe our efforts to encourage tourists should no longer be directed only toward the United States. With London only six hours away by jet and Paris only seven hours from Halifax, I believe we should give some thought to opening a Canadian government travel bureau at least in London and Paris. These places mark the home of our two great cultures which supplied Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific with its settlers, its traditions, its customs and languages.
Our bilingual country offers hospitality to the English or European tourist that cannot be found in the United States or many other countries. We are more accustomed to dealing with this type of tourist, and we do not look upon them as foreigners but appreciate them for what they are. By establishing our historic sites and giving them proper publicity, there is every reason to expect United Kingdom and European tourists to visit Nova Scotia, the province in which the French, English, Scottish and German settlers first landed, as well as other parts of Canada.
Recently we noticed an article in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald, under the heading, "Nova Scotia businessmen find plums aplenty; They've got London talking". The article reads in part:
Nova Scotia businessmen stuck their thumbs into the British business pie this week and pulled out more plums than they had expected.
With less than half the time elapsed before the Halifax-Amherst trade group returns to Canada, many members of the mission feel they have done more than twice as much as they had hoped.
"When you get London talking you've really done something," said Atlantic provinces agent-general Watson Jamer, "and the Canadian businessmen have done just that".
"There's hardly a business in town that isn't aware Nova Scotia is here," he said.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that if we can get these people interested in business, then we can interest them in visiting this country. However, it is up to us to stimulate the interest of these people in visiting the places where their countrymen established settlements in the new world. By so doing we not only strengthen our tourist industry, but we show these tourists a way of life. We want our United States friends and our friends from overseas to see us and become acquainted with the freedom we enjoy as Canadians. We want them to see our institutions of government. In this way, they will acquire a feeling for the spirit of democracy which is of vital importance to all of us and to the peace of the entire world.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
At the outset of my remarks, I should like to say I have no intention of entering into a controversy with my very good friend, the
90205-6-2761
Supply-Northern Affairs hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, who claimed that John Cabot landed at some particular place. We then had an Irishman from Toronto claiming he landed in another place. My views on this matter have been put on the record and I have not changed them since.
In any event, Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the opportunity of making a few remarks during the discussion of the estimates of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources because the economy of my constituency, or a large part of it, is wrapped up in what this department may or may not do, especially in Cape Breton Highlands national park. Like other hon. members of the committee, I should like to express my sincerest congratulations to the new minister upon his appointment. I have no doubt, despite the views that have been expressed to the contrary by the all-wise sage from Port Arthur, he will perform his duties well.
The background of the new minister indicates an awareness of the social problems of our society, and this is indicated by his work during his lifetime. During his early years his abilities and talents were made available, through the Salvation Army, to the inmates of Montreal's Bordeaux jail and St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary. He also performed similar services in Toronto. Later, he served with distinction in the Royal Canadian Air Force and was awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross. His career in politics, including his activities as parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs and now as Minister of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, indicates that he has devoted his life to doing good for his fellow-men. I have no doubt his work as minister of this department will be such that, in the future, we will all be as proud of him as we have been in the past.
Having made that statement, I should like now to bring to the attention of the minister the wage rates that are paid to workers in the Cape Breton park. I brought this matter to the attention of the previous minister, and also to the committee, on several occasions. I should like to report that we have made some small progress. The labour rate at this park is now $1.05 an hour compared with 85 cents an hour before this government came into office. However, as I pointed out on another occasion, this rate is certainly not in keeping with the rates that are paid in the majority of the national parks throughout Canada. It is certainly not a proper wage rate.
As we are all aware, government employee wage surveys are conducted by the Department of Labour at the request of the employing department. I should like to suggest to the minister that the time is past due when

Supply-Northern Affairs a request for another survey should be made.
I would renew my request that when this survey is made consideration be given to the different wage rates that are in effect throughout Cape Breton island and that it be not restricted to the area immediately surrounding the park.
I should like to commend the government, the previous minister and the present minister, for the activities that have been carried out in the park in recent years. The winter works program and the extra work projects that have been carried out in the park have provided a level of employment to my constituents such as they had never experienced in this area previously. I join with my colleague, the hon. member for Inverness-Rich-mond, who remarked the other day in the house that the area concerned has been more prosperous because of the greater amount of work that has been carried out.
In support of this statement, I should like to put on the record the amounts expended in wages at the Cape Breton Highlands national park for the years 1953 to 1960-61. These totals include the salaries of civil servants, prevailing rate employees, and employees on construction work. The years and the amounts expended are in tabulated form, as follows:

This, of course, is completely separate and apart from expenditures made on highway construction in the park. This work which has been carried out means so much to my constituents that I trust it will be continued at a similar rate and expanded to a greater degree if at all possible. I suggest to the minister that this be done.
At the present time great strides are being made in the construction of a large camping ground in the Ingonish area, which I may say is urgently needed to eliminate overcrowding which occurs every year during the tourist season. There is certainly room for further great expansion in this park in many fields.
I must say that of the few recommendations in the recent Rand report with which I agree, two are the recommendations concerning the expansion and development of the Cape Breton Highlands national park, and also the one relating to Fort Louisbourg in the constituency of my colleague from Inverness-Richmond who has been devoting himself so strenuously in this regard.

May I also bring to the attention of the minister the matter of reforestation within the confines of the park. Over a period of years a large portion of the park has been burned over, unfortunately, due to forest fires. I would urge that the minister give consideration to the matter of beautifying the park in the areas where this has occurred.
I realize that the government has in effect a program of financial assistance to the provinces for the purposes of reforestation of vacant crown lands, and in view of this I see no reason why some arrangement could not be worked out in an area such as the park, where it is totally owned by the federal government.
Just recently I brought to the attention of the Minister of Forestry the question of reforestation in Cape Breton. I also brought this to the attention of the Prime Minister, with the thought in mind that, should we eventually have to face the prospect of mine closures, I felt there was no reason why a corps of a couple of hundred of men could not be occupied for a period of up to, say, two years in this type of work.
A program of this nature has been carried out with great success in Great Britain, and I urge the minister to see whether some mutual arrangement could be made whereby this could be carried out in the area I have mentioned.
Another point I should like to draw to the attention of the minister is one that I have discussed with the previous minister and his departmental officials for quite a period of time. That is the question of the historic site at Englishtown and, to be more explicit, Port Dauphin.
At the present time a cairn is located there with the following inscription:
Settled in 1629 by Capt. Charles Daniel and site of an early Jesuit mission selected in 1713 as a naval base and one of the principal places in Isle Royale, named Port Dauphin and strongly fortified. Its importance declined with the choice in 1719 of Louisburg as the capital.
In fact Englishtown is the site of the first permanent white settlement in all Cape Breton and, I am informed, of the first Jesuit mission on the North American continent.
In 1629 a French fort was built at the mouth of Ste. Anne's bay by Captain Daniel of Dieppe. Jesuit priests named the settlement Sainte Anne, in honour of Queen Anne of Austria, the mother of Louis XIV. In 1713 a new fort was built and the place was renamed Fort Dauphin.
I would urge the minister and his departmental officials, to give consideration to the establishment in this area of a national historic park. The historic sites and monuments board, which I understand advise the

minister on the importance of proposed historic sites, have considered this subject on several occasions but have not come to any conclusive decision.
The previous minister advised me that he wished to have the full assurance of the board that Fort Dauphin is of sufficient importance in the broad history of the nation to warrant, in addition to the bronze tablet and cairn already erected there, the establishment of a national historic park.
I understand that this proposition is to appear on the agenda of the board when they hold their meeting next month. I do hope the matter will be gone into very thoroughly at that time and that we will have a favourable decision.
Let me now turn to the question of a new clubhouse for the golf course at the national park. We are fortunate in having one of the finest golf courses in Canada and I only wish I could say that the clubhouse was in keeping with the course.
I brought this question to the attention of the previous minister and, while I realize that tremendous work has been done in the park and that this new construction is receiving every consideration, we have not as yet been successful in having this consideration become a reality.
I would once again urge the minister to go into this matter most thoroughly, and I shall appreciate the opportunity, if he visits the national park this coming summer-and we will certainly welcome him-of taking him on a personal inspection of the clubhouse. I do not think he will be very proud of it.
On a number of occasions I brought to the attention of the previous minister and the department the matter of the restoration of the original Hydrofoil craft, HD4, which was the brainchild of the late Alexander Graham Bell and was the subject of one of his many experiments.
My appeal on those occasions was, of course, for the preservation, restoration and display of this craft. As a result we were very fortunate in that the department made the necessary arrangements and had this relic transported across the Bras d'Or lakes to the locale of the present Bell museum.
However, as yet there is no visible evidence that the restoration will take place, or any evidence of a shelter being constructed so that this craft can be displayed to the many thousands of visitors who visit the museum annually.
I would like the minister to advise me just how soon we can look forward to action being taken along the lines I have suggested, and explain further the reason for the delay. I shall be interested in being provided with any information he has on this project, as it
Supply-Northern Affairs is one well worthy of consideration, mainly because of the fact that it is one of the few objects of this magnitude with which this great man experimented.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I should like to proceed to another subject, and that is the matter of the provision of ski trails at the Cape Breton Highlands national park.
I was pleased to note in the speech from the throne that this government indicated it was interested in the promotion of physical fitness. With this in mind I should like to once again bring to the attention of the minister, as I did to his predecessor, the tremendous benefits which would be derived by having proper ski facilities at the Cape Breton Highlands national park.
I have indicated to the minister in the past just how suitable certain areas of the park, such as South Harbour mountain and several others, would be for the promotion of skiing. It is a sad thing that the tremendous facilities we have available in the park are available only for the short summer season.
Here is an opportunity where great benefit could be derived by the economy of Cape Breton in the introduction of tourist trade during the winter months in the participation of this sport. I can also envisage the labour force that would be needed to prepare these facilities.
There is no doubt at all in my mind that facilities would be provided by the people in the area for the housing accommodation of those interested, should the government take the initiative in establishing the trails and tows.
I understand it has been suggested by departmental officials that there was no object in providing a skiing area since there would be no tourist accommodation available to people who wished to participate in this sport. It is also my understanding that resort owners in the Ingonish area have not taken too kindly to this view, as I feel quite sure they want all the business they can obtain, especially in the winter. Accommodation facilities are there now.
There are a great number of benefits to be derived besides the physical fitness aspect of the proposition. Apart from the money that would be spent on local labour to cut trails and make the necessary skiing facilities, money would also be spent on gasoline, accommodation and meals by visitors to the park who wished to engage in this sport.
It is quite true that large returns could not be expected immediately, but I am sure immediate steps to provide these facilities would reap great rewards in the future.
It is a well known fact that in this part of Nova Scotia there is always more snowfall than anywhere else. Experts in this field have

Supply-Northern Affairs advised me that we have a great potential for this sport in the Cape Breton Highlands national park, so I leave these thoughts with the minister for his consideration. We have the snow, we have the scenery, we have the terrain and we have the interest. All that is needed now is more activity on the part of the department to bring these thoughts into reality. We have excellent highways leading to the park and, indeed, throughout Cape Breton Island as a result of the wonderful co-operation between the Stanfield government of Nova Scotia and this government in the past few years in connection with the roads to resources program. There are also many more highway projects which have been agreed upon by both governments but which are yet to be carried out.
I commend the government on this legislation. It was only this week that ceremonies were held in Cape Breton in connection with the completion of the steel structure of the new bridge across the Bras d'Or lakes. This bridge, costing more than $5 million, was brought about as a result of an agreement between the government of Nova Scotia and the federal government, the federal government paying 90 per cent of the cost and the provincial government paying 10 per cent. When this new bridge, the Robert L. Stanfield bridge, is officially opened in a few months, I suggest that we shall see a greater influx of visitors to the Cape Breton park than ever before and, believe me, their number has been growing enormously every year over the past few years. This in itself is reason enough why the department should develop the park to the greatest possible extent.
Before I resume my seat, may I wish the minister well. I look forward to his visit to the park and I also look forward to seeing some activity along the lines of the proposals I have made. When he replies I trust that he will comment on some of the items I have brought to his attention.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not want to take up too much of the time of the house, but I do wish to set the record straight.
First, I should like to congratulate the new Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Dinsdale). He is endowed with fine qualities, is congenial and is a hard worker. I have seen him at work in several committees, and it was always a pleasure to work with him. I wish him every success in his new department.
In the remarks he made on April 21, the member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm

(Mr. Pigeon) said something that must be corrected, because it does not represent the facts exactly as they are.
After a previous question, he asked the minister what was the language taught to the Eskimos, in addition to their own Eskimo language. The minister replied that for a number of reasons, mainly of an economic nature, it was the English language.
So far so good. Mind you, Mr. Chairman, I am not criticizing the minister I know how difficult these things are. In fact, we cannot always do as we wish very often, our actions are dictated by economic factors, even if we do not exactly like it.
Following that reply, the member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm said this:
Mr. Chairman, may I add that that situation was created and has existed since 1949, in other words, under the Liberal administration of which the member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), as minister of transport, was a member, as was Mr. Jean Lesage, the present premier of Quebec, as minister of northern affairs and national resources and who was therefore chiefly responsible for that situation.
Mr. Chairman, the language taught in northern Canada has always been a problem, and that problem cannot be settled by the present minister any more than it could be by the former minister. Mind you, if the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm was trying to make political capital out of it, I would be the last to blame him.
In fact, I think it is fair and resonable that an hon. member should try to make political capital even in this house. But one must also be generous to abstain from imputing motives to those who are being criticized.
The hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm did not say exactly that the intentions of the Liberal predecessor of the present minister were bad, but he got around the difficulty and implied that the minister did not go too much out of his way and did not try to improve the situation.
Well, we find-and I say so for the benefit of the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm-in the budget discussion on Monday, March 28, 1955, a statement made by the then minister of northern affairs and national resources, Mr. Jean Lesage.
Those projects were discussed at length with bishop Marsh, of the Church of England, and Msgr. Trocellier, of the Catholic church. Both agreed that it is the best program likely to meet the needs in the north and to cope with the difficulties which became greater these last few years because of inadequate school facilities for the children of both religions in the different localities.
We realize, in the light of that text, that the then minister intended to improve the situation.

I am convinced that, even it the present minister does not have much success in this regard, it is not from a lack of good will. In fact, he is one of the hon. members who have always displayed much good will.
Mr. Chairman, I only wanted to stress this: when one makes political hay one must do it carefully so as not to belittle in any way those who used to be in power and who had intended to do right.

speechtext:
As I rise to take part in this debate on the estimates of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources I do so in the spirit of co-operation and in support of what previous members from Nova Scotia have advocated for the betterment of our province so appropriately known as the ocean's playground. I am proud to be from this peninsula-the most weather beaten province of the dominion-one that has stood the test of time. What Nova Scotia lacks in size is more than made up in rugged scenic beauty that so invitingly attracts tourists from other lands.
I was delighted when an invitation was extended to the minister to visit Cape Breton and the Cabot trail. Mention, and rightly so, was made of historical Louisburg. Interesting and varied relics recall here part of Canada's history in its early days and attest to the truth of the fight for supremacy in Canada by two great races. One relives the days of the pioneers' privation and hardships and sees today that all of this was not in vain.
However, in the same spirit that prompted previous Nova Scotia members, and not forgetting that my people think also in terms of equal distribution, and in the knowledge that a fair appraisal cannot be given before all is seen and explored, I open wide to the minister the constituency doors of Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare. Do come on in and browse around and enjoy here the pause that refreshes. I ask him to enter, and I am sure that once he browses around he will indeed find the pause that refreshes.
I need not point out historical facts and events relating to my area of southwestern Nova Scotia. This has been done admirably by the town fathers of Shelburne town. Clare's yearly and colourful Acadian festival vividly succeeds in this historial revival. (Translation):
At this point in my remarks, Mr. Chairman, I would like, with your permission, to pay homage to my friends the Acadians of Baie Ste. Marie. I would like to tell them the high regard in which their yearly festival is held, showing as it does that if they have
Supply-Northern Affairs not entirely forgotten, they have at least forgiven, thus giving a magnificent example to the rest of the world.
(Text):
This year from July 23 to July 29 the Yarmouth "bicenturama" will, after its celebration, leave no doubt in the minds of the visitors fortunate enough to attend, why Yarmouth is called the gateway to the maritimes, and convince those who come to view that they should stay longer than they planned.
We also have natural attractions; nature has seen and still sees to that. We have plenty of trout filled lakes, winding highways and byways, scenery that is rugged and as eye catching as any sea lashed coast in the world, a marine life second to none in the world-in reality a nimrod's delight-a wild life that continues to test and try the skill of sportsmen, amateur and professional. The giant tuna lurks in our waters and still challenges sportsmen from all over the world. Schooling pollock gather close to our shore, frolic and swish in playful fashion at the edge of a turbulent riptide. Oftentimes they seek still waters and in so doing whet the exuberance of youth and stimulate the fading eagerness of the aged.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to believe that the minister agrees that such a setting and tourist attraction should be enhanced by the establishment of a national park. In the nature of suggestion, and wishing to forsake any idea of dictating, I would like to see a marine life display implemented within the confines of a national park. I can assure the minister that our sea coast lends itself admirably well toward this combination of nature's attractions, housed within the sanctuary of a park, to entice greater numbers of tourists to sojourn where perhaps they only intended to linger. At this moment I cannot foresee such a national park housing a marine life display without the presence of the lordly lobster, unconcerned in his migration, taunted by the silvery haddock, shadowed by the silent cod, fearful of the grey seal's acrobatics, and attempting to capture the elusive pollock, all of this viewed by the motionless and almost unseen halibut.
Mr. Chairman, I have indicated what nature has provided us in southwestern Nova Scotia, and I anticipate that the minister will do his share. I should like to indicate what the people there have done for themselves. In the provision of tourist facilities, they have set up many roadside tables, trailer campsites, have built motels and renovated hotels. I am sure that the minister will be most helpful in seeing that these are continually filled to capacity.
I would also like to point out in conclusion that accompanied by what the minister will

Supply-Northern Affairs give us, what our people have provided is the friendly and warm hospitality of a people ambitious to forge ahead and prosper.
