Mr. Chairman, I should like to speak for a few minutes in support of my distinguished friend the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, in respect of the arguments he advanced regarding an appropriate monument to mark the landfall of John Cabot, or John Caboto, depending on the part of the country you hail from.
I would suggest that, by and large, it is time that the government of Canada, with the research, knowledge and advice of its experts, should adjudicate on this controversy, deciding once and for all where the landfall of John Cabot actually was because, in essence, Cabot is the only discoverer of Canada. There are hon. gentlemen sitting in other parts of the house who would debate this subject and who would advance arguments in favour of Jacques Cartier, but I will compromise with those gentlemen, who are welcome to their historical traditions and opinions, by recommending the establishment of a discovery day for Canada and recognition of Jacques Cartier and John Cabot as the co-discoverers. I think hon. members will agree that half a loaf is better than none at all. I do believe, however, that we should honour the day on which these early navigators and adventurers discovered this then unknown land. I think that historic day should be marked appropriately.
The traditional landfall of John Cabot is cape Bonavista, which is in the constituency of my hon. friend opposite. There is substantial historical evidence to support this contention, and I do feel that it at least warrants study and earnest consideration by the historic sites and monuments board. I believe that the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, with the enthusiasm, vigour and earnestness he brings to that department, will see to it that the proper study and attention are given to this subject.
There are those individuals who will say that John Cabot landed at Cape Breton in 1497, but in actual fact the argument in support of that is less than 50 years old. All that one has in support of that argument is a map supposedly drawn or drafted by the son of John Cabot, John Sebastian Cabot. There is at the present time, however, a very earnest study being made of this subject by learned scholars and historians. One learned historian at the university of Miami in the United States has substantial evidence to support the theory that John Cabot did in fact land at Cape Breton, but that several years before his landfall there he had in fact visited the island of Newfoundland. I am sure that in


arguing today in support of the Newfoundland landfall the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate advanced the argument that the name "Bonavista" is derived from the fact that when Cabot, the Genoese navigator and adventurer, sighted the first landfall he is alleged to have said, "O Buena vista", which means "O happy sight". I am sure my learned friend from Bonavista-Twillingate probably said the same thing in 1953

In the vicinity of cape Bonavista there is being developed-it is practically completed-a national park called Terra Nova park. It will certainly supplement the development of this park if consideration were to be given to erecting a monument on cape Bonavista to mark the landfall of what I think and what many people today are coming around to believe was the first landfall of Cabot in what is now known as Canada. In that respect, Mr. Chairman, one would wonder, whether John Cabot landed at cape Bonavista in 1494 or in Cape Breton in 1497, what would go through the mind of this Genoese navigator from Bristol if he were to return to the scene of his triumph some 450 years later? One would wonder what he would find. Well, I have no doubt that the old mariner would be much impressed with what he would find. Perhaps amongst the least significant things he would find would be the fact that there was one who had followed in his footsteps some 450 years later. Perhaps they had a little in common in that Cabot was an adventurer and a navigator from Genoa sailing out of Bristol and Pickersgill was a navigator, and a landlocked navigator sailing out of Manitoba in a prairie schooner.

speechtext:
It gives me the greatest pleasure to congratulate a long time friend of mine, the present minister, who is adding so greatly to the cabinet by his heading of this important department. He is a man who,

while aggressive and able, is also agreeable and is entertained in high regard by hon. members in this house. 1 look forward to great things from the new minister; among those a greater impetus in the program with respect to the international peace garden between Manitoba and North Dakota in the riding of Brandon-Souris.
I heard my colleagues from the province of Nova Scotia inviting the minister to come down and visit them. One member wants him to go skiing in Cape Breton and another member wants him to come across the south shore. It was suggested that he might go to the places that Cabot visited, although there is some difference of opinion as to what those actually were. Before he was minister I was fortunate enough to have the hon. gentleman come to Prince Edward Island and he was good enough to launch my campaign in 1956. I look forward to his return. If he returns he will find that in the years since 1956 because of certain changes which have taken place in Ottawa and in Charlottetown that Prince Edward Island generally is an even more beautiful place than it was at that time.
I listened to the learned and hon. gentlemen discuss history tonight. I am not going away back into historical researches; I am going to talk only about the tourist business. In Prince Edward Island, of course, we consider that Jacques Cartier was our first tourist. I go back only as far as 1534 when that great man was in our province. He stopped there and he said it was not only the fairest land that he had ever seen but indeed one could not conceive of a fairer. He referred to certain other parts of what is now Canada as probably being the land that God gave to Cain, but he did not say that about Prince Edward Island. He was our first and one of our most appreciative visitors from Europe.
The department which the minister heads has contributed in no small measure to the improvement in our economy and indeed in our spirits in Prince Edward Island, which I mentioned just a moment ago. The roads to resources program has stimulated the greatest highway construction program that Prince Edward Island has ever known in its long history. We are proud of the fact that-I hope my hon. friend from Cape Breton North and Victoria will not take exception to this-the Prince Edward Island national park tops all other parks in Canada in the increase in tourists in the last year. We had over 412,000 people come to that beautiful park on the north side of Prince Edward Island and the north side of Queens county. For many years the national park stood there. A program of development was seemingly much retarded.

I can say that while the number of visitors to the province of Prince Edward Island is increasing, the province is able to look after them well and they will be welcomed. We will do an even better job if the Minister of Public Works will construct a causeway because they will come to us so much more quickly. Perhaps this is not the time to go into that matter, nor is this the department under which to discuss it.
I think the minister can look with satisfaction upon the results in my province of the campsite program. We have had many new developments on some beautiful sites. I think this is a splendid program and I would commend to the minister, lest he think that I am incapable of suggesting that there are areas within his department capable of being improved, that perhaps the campsite program might easily be geared to the roads to resources program and not exclusively to the trans-Canada highway.
I do not know how many hon. members know that much of the increase in tourist activity in recent years in the Atlantic provinces stems from the excellent and special program of the Canadian government travel bureau. The recent setting aside of $300,000 for special advertising in the eastern states, with emphasis upon the Atlantic provinces, has borne great fruit. I think the suggestion that has been offered by the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg for a heavier concentration of activity in this connection in the United Kingdom is a good one. We rejoice in the Atlantic provinces that just a year ago Halifax was linked in direct T.C.A. contact with the United Kingdom. This will prevent the unfortunate tendency that sometimes prevails when visitors from the United Kingdom and Europe make a visit to Canada. Often they started in Montreal and moved westward. This is now no longer necessary.
A special project of much interest to me is the Fort Amherst historic park. Prince Edward Island has an interesting history under French occupation and then early days as an English colony and many years as a province in confederation. The site of Port Lajoie and Fort Amherst is specially suited for a park. I commend them for developing it. I realize that these projects have a great archaeological historical development and much study, but I would suggest that even though the site has lain there for a couple of centuries without development that perhaps even though it is an historic spot, a

I was almost tempted to follow the line of some of the learned speakers who have preceded me and I think it is commendable we have given some time to a discussion and appraisal of, and perhaps even disagreement over, our historic sites. Many Nova Scotians have spoken tonight. I should like to put on the record the words of one of the greatest Nova Scotians who began as a Liberal and ended, I think you might say, as a Conservative. I refer not to the great Sir Robert Borden who did the same thing but to an earlier man, Joseph Howe, who said:
A wise nation preserves its records, gathers up its muniments, decorates the tombs of its illustrious dead, repairs its great public structures, and fosters national pride and love of country, by perpetual reference to the sacrifices and glories of the past.
We have done so tonight. We have gone back to Cabot, Jacques Cartier, Leif Ericsson and Eric the Red. I can only say that very soon in Prince Edward Island we are going back in a similar way to 1864. I hope that when the minister is through travelling in Nova Scotia

my colleagues there are going to keep him busy because they are suggesting national parks here and there-he will come to Prince Edward Island for a rest. Our province is small. Mr. Chairman, when I last spoke on these estimates I indicated there were two other sectors of the northern economy that I wanted to cover before the first item was passed. On April 21 I dealt with the question of the political development of the Yukon particularly and now I want to deal with the material and resource development of the north.
While I have been very interested in the remarks maritime members have made tonight concerning the development of national parks, tourism and the like, I believe the committee is glossing over the main activity of the department in the development of what constitutes 40 per cent of the territory of our nation. The material and resource development of the northern portions of Canada are most important to the future national economic growth of this country. These regions are rich beyond measure in natural resources, in mineral products for which demand is growing throughout the whole world day by day. Rare minerals are being required in ever-increasing quantities by those engaged in the race for outer space.
For the purpose of organizing the efficient search for and development of the mineral resources of the north, one of the most vital sectors in which the department should be interesting itself, and I am sure the minister is aware of this, is the field of research. I have spoken on previous occasions in the

house this session about the need for northern research. The need of a co-ordinated research program in the north is very vital to research development which ultimately will benefit the whole nation.
The need of research in the field of transportation is one of the most vital sectors on which the department should be focusing its attention. One of the more urgent requirements is a complete assessment of the transportation needs of the Mackenzie river watershed in the Northwest Territories. Transportation problems in this area are rapidly developing to a point where they are going to cause real difficulties from the point of view of the requirements of the area. The research efforts of the federal departments should be directed toward the field of communication and navigation systems in the north generally, particularly telephone and telegraph communications, railroads and radio. New methods of transportation and new methods of communication are vital to orderly development in these northern regions.
The development of new types of transportation vehicles such as the Letourneau Monster, is one early result of scientific ingenuity in this field. I believe there are even more startling vehicles and modes of transportation on the drawing boards today. There should be some co-ordination of effort in the gathering of information on the manufacturing of tires and equipment, information now available in the armed forces, information which has been garnered by soldiers, airmen and naval personnel who have had experience in these regions. There should be co-ordination of information which has been gathered by research agencies, engine manufacturers and the like; research in the field of transportation systems, economic routes and load analyses. I believe the department should take the lead here in co-ordinating the efforts of the Department of Transport, the armed forces, the railroad industries and of transportation consultants generally.
In other words, there should be research, first in the selection and integration of existing forms of travel in the north, on land, sea, air, rail and pipe line. It is not inconceivable that the oil resources of the north will perhaps one day be transported by means of some sort of plastic pipe line. The British have made great strides in this field by towing a sort of plastic sausage in which oil products are carried behind a submarine. The efforts of the Department of Transport and those of the Department of National Defence should be co-ordinated and related in this field. There should be research into the climate, terrain, exploration methods, survey methods. There should be research into soil mechanics and 90205-6-277i
Supply-Northern Affairs terradynamics, power generation, atomic power, hydro, thermal and diesel.
It is interesting to note that progress has been made by the Soviet union in the field of research in these sectors. I should like to quote from the Soviet news bulletin, which is undated but of recent vintage, an article concerned with northern research. I quote:
Gordon Robertson, Canada's deputy minister of northern affairs and national resources in his speech to parliament said that "the U.S.S.R. is ahead of Canada in the development of the northern regions, and it is high time for us to admit it. Soviet union engages in vast research work in the north. U.S.S.R. has done more in this respect than all the countries of the world put together." The symposium on the problems of development of Canada's northwestern regions of 1958, stressed the need of assimilating from the Russians the principle of planning in solving the questions of development of the northern areas.
The article continues in a like vein. I believe we have a good deal to learn from the Russian efforts in the north. At the risk of being quoted in the Soviet news bulletin, I would suggest that it might prove useful if the minister were to arrange for the freest possible exchange of information between the officials of his department and those engaged in similar efforts in the Soviet union. I think we could learn a good deal from the efforts of the Soviet union, and I am sure they could learn a good deal from our own efforts in the north.
One of the newest institutes of an academic nature to make its entry into the field has been the Boreal institute of the university of Alberta. The object of this recently formed institute is to do research along the same lines as that of the Arctic institute which has its headquarters, as the minister knows, in Montreal. One of the objects of the Boreal institute, which incidentally is prepared to make a go of it on an initial capital of $10,000, is to provide an information centre, training and inspection, and to undertake, co-ordinate and administer research in the north. I have a statement of the objectives of the Boreal institute which I shall be glad to pass along to the minister if he has not a copy of it, as I suspect he has. Institutes like these are very deserving of the support of the federal government by way of grants to further this very necessary and vital work to the future economic benefit of Canada.

speechtext:
I want to turn for just a moment to the material concerning resources development in the Yukon and Northwest Territories and the expenditures on the development of roads and bridges in those two areas. The Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources during the years 1952 and 1957 spent the sum of $2.5 million in the Yukon and $1,150,000 in the Northwest Territories for these objects. During the period 1957-1962 over $16 million was spent in the Yukon Territory and $20 million in the Northwest Territories, so it can readily be seen that the comparison between the two periods is quite startling.
The point I wish to make in connection with these expenditures is simply this, that
[The Deputy Chairman.]
whereas from reaching a point six years ago where virtually no development was taking place in these northern regions-which development, I submit to the hon. member and his colleagues opposite, is very, very beneficial to the future economy of this nation-there is now a substantial development taking place.
The Leader of the Opposition and other hon. members opposite have very often taken issue with the northern development policies of this government. The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo last Friday became quite emotional on this point and said that all these plans had been laid by the previous administration.
The hon. member for Richelieu-Yercheres has said this in the past, as has the Leader

of the Opposition. These hon. members have said that all the plans were laid by the previous administration and all that was being done was that this government was carrying them into effect. In effect they were saying, "These were our plans. We should get the credit for this. We are all for this road development program. We are all for the blossoming forth of the north as a resource reservoir for the nation.
I think these gentlemen should get together with the leader of their party, for I can recall that on several occasions in 1958 their leader ridiculed the plans of the government with regard to northern development. These hon. members ridiculed speeches which our Prime Minister was making across the country and which the Leader of the Opposition was ridiculing just as fast as he followed the Prime Minister's campaign trail across the country.
In Swift Current, on February 27, 1958, the Leader of the Opposition classed these roads as "roads from igloo to igloo". This is the famous "igloo to igloo" statement.
I am sure the Leader of the Opposition, as well as all hon. members opposite, will be happy to know that this particular road which was classed as one from igloo to igloo is now approaching the site of the first oil well which was brought in in the Yukon Territory in 1959; and another oil well is being drilled now in the same area.
I am sure, too, that the same critics of this road program will be happy to know that as a direct result of this program there has been discovered on the boundary of the Yukon-Northwest Territories, at a place called Flat river, the world's largest known tungsten deposit, a deposit which it is anticipated will be sufficient to supply the whole of the considerable United States' demands for tungsten, a very strategic metal in these days of space achievement and space striving.
I can recall another statement having been made by the Leader of the Opposition. This was in Vancouver on September 27, 1958, when he said:
Diefenbaker's promise of a billion dollar public works program in the Arctic is the phoniest promise ever made in Canadian history.
I think the statistics I have tabled will show that, far from being the phoniest promise in Canadian history, it has proved to be the most realistic achievement of any government in Canadian history.
Contrast it with an average annual expenditure of all federal government departments, for the period 1952 to 1957, of $46 million in the Northwest Territories and $36 million in the Yukon Territory. In the same
Supply-Northern Affairs period of years, 1957 to 1962, in the Northwest Territories $156 million will be expended; and in the Yukon Territory, $79,916,888, which is almost $80 million. Therefore when I said that all federal departments had increased their expenditures fivefold, I was not too far out in my estimation.
I wish to deal for a moment with the minister's announcement yesterday of the assistance program which his department is planning in the construction and maintenance of access roads to stimulate exploration, prospecting and development of the mineral resources of the north.
This is a very necessary policy which the government has very wisely adopted. This should be contrasted with the policy of the previous government, which was, "You show us that you have a resource; show us that you have an ore body that is worthy of development and we will build the road. There will be no assistance in road building until you can prove to our satisfaction that you have an ore body that has been proven."
Mr. Chairman, this is putting the cart before the horse, because in order to develop the resources of this vast area in the north there must be a stimulus given to exploration and prospecting. The only way that stimulus will come about is for the government to be interested financially in the field of resource exploration.
Before I leave the subject of roads, Mr. Chairman, I should like to remind the minister that he has a study under way concerning the all-weather maintenance of the Haines cut-off. I should like the minister to comment at some stage during the discussion of his estimates on the results of this survey, if they are yet available, because I believe the maintenance of the Haines cut-off as an all-weather road is essential to efficient resource development in the Yukon territory.
I should also very urgently press the minister to consider carrying out an engineering survey, and an economic survey which should perhaps precede the engineering survey, of a highway link between Carcross and Skagway. This has been discussed by many organizations in the Pacific northwest, not only in the Yukon, as an essential link in order to effectively develop the resources of the area.
The other matter I wish to discuss before I leave the subject of resources generally is that of changes in the Yukon Quartz Mining Act and the Yukon Placer Mining Act. As the minister has explained in the house on more than one occasion, the Canada mining regulations which were recently passed do not apply to the Yukon territory.
I well recall reading about the effort that was made by the previous administration to

Supply-Northern Affairs alter the Yukon Quartz Mining Act so as to include the power to make regulations under that act. The member for the Yukon at the time-the Liberal member for the Yukon at the time, I may say-moved that the bill which was introduced by Mr. Lesage not be read a second time. He was supported in that motion by the now Secretary of State for External Affairs.
I urge the minister, in considering any alterations to the Yukon Quartz Mining Act and the Yukon Placer Mining Act, to have the fullest and most complete discussions with the mining fraternity and the mining industry in the Yukon territory. Also, the Yukon legislative council, which speaks for the people there, as their own local legislature, is a competent body capable of assessing the effect of any contemplated changes in this legislation. It would be a very sad thing indeed if any move were made to alter these two existing pieces of legislation which now guarantee to the mining people in the Yukon territory a set of rules which they understand and to which they adhere in their efforts to develop mineral resources.
I want to say a brief word about tourism in the north and to commend the department for the large support which it is giving to the Klondike festival at Dawson city, a project which is being organized by the Klondike festival foundation at Dawson city, the main planning being directed by Mr. Tom Patterson who was the founder of the Stratford festival. The date of the Klondike festival has been set for 1962 and it is expected the event will double or triple tourist travel in this area of Canada.
I should like the minister to bring the committee up to date concerning the plans which have been evolved for the establishment of a national park in the Yukon territory. I know the department had plans and I know that the idea was submitted to the Yukon legislative council and has been considered by them, but I am not aware of the recent departmental thinking along these lines.
I feel, too, that the minister and his department should take the lead in the formation of a public utilities commission in the Yukon territory. I am not aware whether there is a public utilities commission in the Northwest Territories but I can tell the minister that there is no such commission in the Yukon. This has brought about a situation where there is a possibility of rates which are abusive being charged by public utilities in the area. I am not suggesting that this is the case at the moment. The rates charged by the electrical utility in Whitehorse have, indeed, been reduced recently but it is possible that if the minister were to use his good
[Mr. Nielsen.1
offices to encourage the establishment of a utilities commission a much greater control could be exercised in this regard.
Another area in which I feel the time has long passed for action concerns the establishment of a securities commission in the Yukon Territory so that these fly by night promoters will be precluded from forming spurious companies and selling spurious stock to unsuspecting buyers on the basis of resource developments in the north. I am sure all hon. members have heard of the famous Mr. Cal-dough who was extradited from England and who is now in Vancouver charged with fraud arising from the sale of spurious stock. It is interesting to note that Mr. Caldough's basis for the sale of these stocks was property in the oil development areas of the Yukon Territory. This is a very great omission in the Yukon. I think this is the only area in Canada which is now without the protection I have suggested.
These remarks conclude what I have to say concerning resource development in the north, and I am left with only one sector to cover. I should like to do this before the first item passes. It deals with human development. At the pleasure of the committee I will speak at another time on this item, or I can proceed now. I shall be about another 15 minutes.

maintopic: FEDERAL REVENUE FROM OIL AND GAS
speechtext: The hon. member for Yukon always makes a useful contribution to our debates and I think this is the appropriate time to ask him a question. I did not do so while he was speaking. As I understood him, he began by saying, as the burden of his argument, that the new government was doing things in the policy field different from those which had been done by the previous government. In support of that contention I think he referred simply to the fact that certain items of expenditure have been greater since the new government took office. I wonder if the hon. member would indicate to us what new policies have been introduced since the change of administration irrespective of expenditure on old policies such as he was discussing?

maintopic: FEDERAL REVENUE FROM OIL AND GAS
speechtext:
I should be very glad to do that. There are two important sectors, and the first one is this. Our future in the north is bound to be a mining future. I think that is agreed. The policy of the previous government with respect to development roads was this; "You prove to us that you have an ore body capable of being developed, and we shall assist you in building a road." That policy has been reversed and the government is now building roads into potential resource areas without requiring any evidence of there being proven ore bodies there. It is doing this in order to develop the area generally. It is

taking a gamble, whereas the previous government was certainly not taking any risk. The point I make is that the gamble has paid off, and paid off very substantially.

maintopic: FEDERAL REVENUE FROM OIL AND GAS
speechtext: The hon. member has not said where. What about the Pine Point railway proposition?

maintopic: FEDERAL REVENUE FROM OIL AND GAS
speechtext: Well, that was, of course, a proposition which was thought of by the previous administration and it is now being built by this government.

maintopic: FEDERAL REVENUE FROM OIL AND GAS
speechtext: It is not started yet and we have unemployment.

maintopic: FEDERAL REVENUE FROM OIL AND GAS
speechtext:
There is no difference in basic policy there, because there are proven resources already in that area. But the hon. member asked me a specific question concerning a difference in policy. This difference is very real and it is producing real results because whereas formerly there was nothing spent by the previous administration on speculative roads, which is what they are, the country is now being opened up on a large scale. Of course, this government would have been in very serious trouble if this policy had not paid off. The point is that it has paid off as anyone with faith in the north would realize it must pay off. I am happy to say that whereas Canada did not produce an ounce of tungsten, for instance, except in very special circumstances during the war, a new tungsten mine will open up in the Northwest Territories in 1962 which will be the world's largest single supplier of this product. This mine was discovered as a direct result of the policy of road building to which I have referred.
With the permission of the committee I will pass very briefly to the last section of my remarks. I want to cover the sector of human development in the north. When the statistics which I have put on record in Hansard are read by hon. members it will be realized that in the field of education very substantial increases have been made in the grants for the establishment of schools and for participation in educational developments in the north generally. I am very happy to see that this educational assistance has been extended with federal concurrence to the field of separate schools in the north as well.
Great strides have been made in the field of housing. Just how great they are can best be realized if I tell the members of the committee that before 1957 not one single dwelling unit had been constructed in the Yukon territory under the provisions of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, not because the people were not there to build them but because the terms of legislation were unworkable. In 1958 there was one
Supply-Northern Affairs building, in 1959 there were 16 buildings, and in 1960 there were 32 buildings. There are some 50 to 60 buildings under construction at the present time. These figures point out very dramatically the strides that have been made in this regard.

maintopic: FEDERAL REVENUE FROM OIL AND GAS
speechtext: There has been a 1 per cent increase in interest to the purchaser since the former administration.

maintopic: FEDERAL REVENUE FROM OIL AND GAS
speechtext:
I am not an expert on interest rates as the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River is, and I should not like to get into an argument with him regarding rates of interest. I do know that where none were built before, we have now 50 units a year going up in that area.
The other matter on which I should like to have the minister give me current information, has regard to the scheme for the development of lot 19 at Whitehorse, and the establishment of a home builders' loan fund for the people of the Yukon territory who desire to build their own homes.
There are one or two other very brief items I should like to draw to the minister's attention. The first is a matter which I have been asked to present by the miners of the Yukon territory concerning the question of income tax and workmen's compensation. Recently the international union of mine, mill and smelter workers of the Yukon, local 924, made a certain submission to the Yukon legislative council concerning the reduction in income tax, or rather an increase in the basic exemption allowed under taxing legislation. These submissions resulted in a motion made in the Yukon legislative council during their last session to the effect that all bona fide residents of the Yukon in the single category, not otherwise subsidized by the federal government, be given an additional tax exemption of $500; and second, that all bona fide residents of the Yukon in the married category, not otherwise subsidized by the federal government be given an additional exemption of $1,000 on their tax; and third, that all bona fide residents of the Yukon building their own private residences be allowed to depreciate these homes as a deductible item in respect of their tax.
I know this matter has been presented to this house under the previous administration. The reason advanced in support of this contention, which I am very grateful to learn is favoured by the deputy minister of the department, can best be summed up from the journals. It is set forth as follows:
-that to encourage people to stay in the Yukon, to create the permanency of settlement necessary to the full development of the north, certain inequalities in living costs as well as housing facilities will need to be adjusted. The large mining companies recognize this fact and to an extent subsidize housing for their employees. The

Supply-Northern Affairs federal government also recognizes this added cost of living in the Yukon and subsidizes their employees by virtue of the isolated post allowance.
Then follows the resolution. I put this forward again for the minister's consideration, and perhaps the treasury board will take another look at the problem. I understand they have been the stumbling block in the past.
The question of workmen's compensation is a local problem but it is under the minister's jurisdiction in the sense that, as he knows, the same board that handles Yukon compensation cases handles the Northwest Territories compensation cases. For a long time the labour element in my constituency have been advocating a separate board for the Yukon territory so that claimants can be more expeditiously and fairly dealt with by a board which could assess claims on the spot.
I realize the committee has been very fair with me in allowing me to go over my allotted time in covering this rather large field. I should not have thought I would impose upon the committee to the extent I have, but had the hon. member for Mackenzie River been with us during the discussion of these estimates I perhaps would not have taken so much time. I have tried to be as non-partisan as I know he would have been, and I am sure he would support me in the submissions I have made concerning the Nothwest Territories in particular and the north generally. I should like to thank the committee for its courtesy.

maintopic: FEDERAL REVENUE FROM OIL AND GAS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I thank the hon. member for Yukon for his statement and would ask him if I am right or wrong in assessing his statement when I say that he has suggested the difference between the former administration and the present administration is that the present administration would build a road irrespective of the economic report, on the grounds of providing additional employment without regard to the existence of a mine at the end of the road, or whether the project promised success or not. Is that what the hon. member has said?

maintopic: FEDERAL REVENUE FROM OIL AND GAS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have said quite the contrary of that. I said the former administration insisted upon knowing there was a mine at the other end of the road before it would even undertake to invest a penny in the project. For instance, I know that a submission was made to the former administration for building a winter road to the oil fields at Eagle Plain in the Yukon. This request was rejected because it was not in conformity with the policy of the former administration. In contrast to that policy the government is building a highway into this area which will carry all-weather traffic.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. G. Dinsdale (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: FEDERAL REVENUE FROM OIL AND GAS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think you will agree that this has been a wide ranging discussion. As I pointed out in the brief opening statement, the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources covers a wide range of fields. On the whole the discussion has been carried on a positive note, for which I should like to express my thanks to all hon. members who have contributed to the discussion in presenting many useful ideas during the course of the debate.
I am not going to take up the time of the committee by answering each point, but I assure hon. members that every point that has been raised during the course of this rather wide ranging discussion will be answered in the form of a letter.
One of the recurring items in the discussion, and this is of course inevitable, has been the question regarding who is responsible for the present pace of modern development. I do not intend to become involved in this subject tonight, other than by underlying the fact that, as the new Minister of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, during the course of an extensive tour of all parts of the Arctic, which concluded last week end with a trip to the eastern Arctic ranging from Cambridge bay to Frobisher bay, I was tremendously impressed by the rapid pace of development and progress of Canada's Arctic. I think I should merely say that what I have seen has demonstrated to me, more effectively and dramatically than ever before, that Canada is a northern nation, with a northern economy and a northern destiny.
Fortunately, Mr. Chairman, a good many of the queries raised during the discussion have already been answered by the various hon. members who have spoken, and I refer particularly to the hon. member for the Yukon.
There was one particularly critical note during the discussion, and I should like to refer to it briefly in passing. I do so very kindly, because I am a teacher myself and I understand that when my hon. friend from Port Arthur made his references there was nothing personal involved. He is just one of those petulant pedagogues who view the scene from Mount Olympus which gives rise to the statement from time to time that those who can, do; those who cannot, teach. I do not agree with that statement because, being a member of the teaching profession myself, I know there are many in this profession who have made outstanding contributions in a practical and positive way as well as their contribution to the academic world.

Perhaps I have some helpful advice for the hon. member here this evening. I know there is nothing malicious or personal in his statements because in the current issue of Maclean's magazine he makes precisely the same statements regarding the group to which he belongs. I quote from page 26 the following words:
Fisher's own party has not been immune to his critical darts. Shortly after the C.C.F. and the Canadian Labour Congress got their new party project under way, Fisher calmly told the Ontario convention of the C.C.F. that the party's tactics had been stupid and its strategy bad.
I do not think the remarks in reference to myself were as pointed as these observations. The article goes on to point out the difficulty, and it is here where I wish to be helpful. I go on to quote the hon. member as follows:
All my life I've been searching for someone to look up to but my experience has always been to move from respect, almost awe, through understanding to a mild jeer. In the army, I thought I was involved in a great purpose, and then I realized that rank had almost no relation to ability. At university, I ended up completely disrespectful of most professors.

maintopic: FEDERAL REVENUE FROM OIL AND GAS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, far be it from me to rise on a point of order, and I appreciate this publicity but as to its relevancy to the department I should like an explanation from the minister before he continues.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: FEDERAL REVENUE FROM OIL AND GAS
speechtext:
1 shall come to that point in one moment. I continue with the quotation:
When I came to Ottawa, I thought I would at last find giants before whom I could stand in perennial respect. But I found no permanent idols here.
Therefore, if I could quote scripture, he has discovered that all his idols have feet of clay, which is the case in most human circumstances. But here is where I wish to be helpful, and here is where I become quite germane to the discussion under way. The hon. member was kind enough to make reference to a very important conference, namely the resources for tomorrow conference, which is scheduled for Montreal next October. I believe his was the only reference to the conference, and it provides me with an opportunity during the present discussion to underline the importance and the significance of the conference. He pointed out the fact that there had been a lack of suitable publicity. I hope this is not true because we have been successful in getting together a most qualified secretariat headed by a man of established reputation in the resources development field which for the past several months have been working early and late, in season and out of season, in order to get this conference under way. If there has been any neglect regarding publicity I think it might be on the part of hon. members themselves.
Supply-Northern Affairs
This parliament has a very important function and role to play in the promotion of the resources for tomorrow conference. There is no partisanship in this conference. It comes from the realization that the time is long past due when Canadians should get together the best brains, the people most qualified, and give serious consideration to the future development of our renewable resources.
The secretariat responsible for organizing the conference have issued bulletins which have been placed in the hands of all hon. members and if, as the hon. member for Port Arthur suggests, there are local publicity media in his constituency which have not heard of the conference I think it is easy to conclude where the difficulty lies. To the best of our ability and with all the means at our disposal we must all do our best to make this conference an outstanding success.
There is another point about the conference that I should like to mention. This is a cooperative venture between the federal and provincial governments. In planning for this conference there was no suggestion of precedence of one governmental level. It is a partnership among all levels of government. Those sitting on the steering committee are actually representative of the provincial and federal authorities, but also the municipal bodies have a responsibility in assisting in the promotion of this conference. There is no thought of a federal and a provincial conflict in this conference; it is a complete partnership all down the line, and this is exactly the way we want it to continue. Therefore, if my hon. friend is looking for a cause to pursue, looking for an idol, is in pursuit of the summum bonum, or the holy grail, there is something that he can give his attention to and in so doing make a contribution that will redound to posterity.
There was also some observation to the effect that nothing very much is going on in the north. I will not labour that point at all because what has been said in discussion already has more than refuted this point, but here is a field in which the hon. member for Port Arthur might be able to make an outstanding contribution. He is an educationist of some considerable repute. One of the programs that we are proudest of in the north is our rapid progress in education. Just three years ago 16 per cent of our own Eskimo children were in schools. Today that percentage has reached the 60 per cent level and we hope that within the next four years every Eskimo child will have the advantage of an education similar to that of any other Canadian child.
If as the hon. member for Port Arthur has indicated he does not feel he is making

Supply-Northern Affairs a worth-while contribution in the house, I should like to suggest that there is tremendous scope in our educational program in the north, and we would be glad to welcome him into our program when he retires from this honourable house. I am sure he would find that in the north there is a real challenge that would test the mettle of the best of us.
There was another suggestion that the work of the committee on mines, forests and waters has been an exercise in futility and that nothing ever emerges from the committee. I should like to recite briefly the recommendations that have already been implemented during the past three years as a result of the deliberations of the committee. Water problems have been dealt with. There were 11 main recommendations and all except one have been implemented. The Nelson river system study that was recommended is in process at the present time. The idea of a long distance national power grid is under active study at the moment. The field of water pollution and abatement has been dealt with in legislation that was passed in the house last fall. Various water development programs such as the upper Thames program, the Parkhill dam and Ausable river conservation program are in process, and just the other day it was my privilege to announce co-operation with other authorities in the metro Toronto conservation plan.
The new forestry department which was recommended by the committee is now a fact. Travel bureau activities have been expanded, as has been indicated by various speakers during the course of the debate, and this year we are opening a new office in San Francisco. The productivity council, of course, was also an idea that came out of the deliberations of this important committee.
I could go on with other points. There is just one more I should like to mention. The hon. member for Port Arthur quoted from our official bulletin to the effect that morale was in a rather low state in the Mackenzie delta region, but he did not complete the quotation. It is quite true that this has been one of our most difficult areas because of the lack of resources but it is also one of the most encouraging areas for economic development at the present time, and if he had been completely objective academically in his presentation to the house he would have read the final sentence which is in these words:
As a result, a program of Improved resource harvesting will be started during 1960 leading to a more effective use of fish and sea mammals, the production of locally produced dog food, a logging program for housing, and the development of handicrafts and fur garments for commercial sale in the south.
[Mr. Dinsdale.l
This program is under way at the present time. I had the opportunity of seeing it in operation when I was in this area during the Easter recess.
Perhaps I might refer briefly to some of the other points raised. I could spend a long time dealing with the points raised by the hon. member for Yukon. He is most knowledgeable in this field and many times I go to him for advice and information when we are considering the problems of the north. There are just a few references I should perhaps make. He raised a query about a statement I was supposed to have made on the prospects of a new province north of the 60th parallel. I should merely like to say that I agree entirely with the view he expressed. This depends wholly on the increase in population and on the rapidity of development of the economy of the north. I say that from experience because my own province of Manitoba was carved out of the Northwest Territories and had to await the influx of population after the construction of the C.P.R. and the resultant economic development before it could be declared a separate province within confederation. We are anticipating the same process in the north. How long or how short it will be will depend entirely on the rate of progress and development of that important territory.

speechtext: Before the minister leaves that point, may I say that he was fixed by the C.B.C. with a statement to the effect that he was advocating the joinder of the Mackenzie river district and the Yukon as a province. That is the point that has to be cleared up.

From the standpoint of history and tradition and all other considerations that would be quite impossible because the Yukon is the Yukon and the Northwest Territories are the Northwest Territories and never the twain shall meet in interprovincial co-operation. hands of the members of that governing body. 1 think I shall leave his other points to be dealt with by correspondence and in personal discussion. I do express my appreciation to the hon. member for having brought these matters to my attention.

Moyie, and are seeking ways and means to preserve this historic old relic. I could refer to other matters raised by the hon. member. I was very interested in the comments made by the maritime members who were most energetic and enthusiastic in presenting the viewpoint of that important part of Canada. If I were to refer to the remarks of each hon. member I am sure it would take more time than I have at my disposal tonight. I am fully aware that the maritime provinces have rich resources both from the standpoint of tourism and the standpoint of national parks and historic sites. We have various projects under way at the moment. That is my reason for making a tour of the mari-times this summer. Supply-Northern Affairs
The hon. member for Nipissing spent some time discussing the tourist industry. I merely want to say in passing that we have no reason to be pessimistic about progress in tourism in Canada. Just two weeks ago I received the official statistics for the past tourist season and they indicated that, for the first time, the tourist industry became the second largest dollar earner in the Canadian economy. For the first time, the tourist industry was ahead of wheat. Newsprint was first, tourist receipts second and wheat third. Progress is being made so rapidly in this industry that I am convinced it will not be long until tourism will occupy first position. I believe the maritime provinces will be the area where this will occur first.
As a final word on this subject of tourism, I should like to say that the expenditure of the tourist dollar in Canada has been going up. It is true that Canadians have been expending an increasing amount of money in the United States as well. We cannot compare the two and say that the deficit has been increasing. This is a relative thing, and if measured in these terms, we have every reason to be optimistic.
I shall not enter the discussion about Cabot and where he first landed or who has priority in that respect. I will just make this comment, that after hearing the Irishman in full flight tonight, I can only conclude that the sweetest recollections of life are memories of things forgotten. This is the only comment I wish to make on this important subject here tonight.
Having covered these few points, Mr. Chairman, I shall let the matter rest. If there are any further questions, I am sure hon. members can raise them as we proceed to the various items in the estimates.

I am sure the opposition is looking forward to next week with the same interest. Tomorrow we will continue, and I presume complete, the estimates of this very interesting and important Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. We will then continue with the estimates of the Department of Fisheries.
For next week, Monday and Tuesday will be a supply motion. I think it is No. 5 in the list of supply motions. For the balance of the week, so that hon. members may make the necessary preparations, it is likely that on the estimates side the following departments will be before the house, national revenue, justice, mines and technical surveys, and forestry. However, I will give a more precise outline tomorrow of the order in which those estimates will come.
Does the minister think that is enough estimates?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: With the desire of the house to complete early in June, I feel sure I should add another department to that list.
Veterans affairs.
I wonder whether I could ask the house leader if he has any report about the railway situation?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
No. I have just heard rumours; I have no official report.
